A bedside co-sleeper crib attached to the family bed can give grandparents and parents close proximity and easy access for night feeds while keeping the baby on their own firm sleep surface.
What risk factors make bed-sharing especially dangerous?

The AAP identifies smoking by any adult in the bed (even if they do not smoke during the sleep period), consumption of alcohol or sedating medication, extreme fatigue, a soft or water mattress, loose pillows and duvets, and prematurity or low birth weight as factors that substantially increase the danger of bed-sharing. When any of these factors apply, the risk of SIDS or sleep-related death is considerably higher than the already elevated baseline.
Does UNICEF support any form of co-sleeping?

UNICEF UK acknowledges that bed-sharing is widely practised and provides a safer bed-sharing guide (the Seven Cs) for families who choose to do so, while maintaining that a separate sleep surface in the same room is always the safest option. Their position is harm-reduction focused: if families are going to share a sleep surface, they should know the conditions that reduce risk as far as possible.

d.t: Co-sleeping: traditions, safety and what the evidence says
q: Is bedsharing always dangerous?

Bedsharing carries the highest risk on soft surfaces (sofas, armchairs), when either parent has consumed alcohol or sedating drugs, or when the baby was born premature or at low birthweight. In lower-risk settings, on a firm flat mattress, with no duvets near the baby and no smoking in the household, the absolute risk is much smaller, though it is never zero. The safest sleep surface for a baby remains a firm, flat, separate surface in the same room as a caregiver.
How long should my baby sleep in my room?

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends room-sharing (baby on a separate surface in the same room) for at least the first six months, and ideally for the first year. UK NHS guidance is consistent with this. Room-sharing reduces SIDS risk compared to sleeping in a separate room.
What is a sidecar cot arrangement?

A sidecar cot is a cot or bassinet placed right beside the parent's bed, with one side removed or lowered so the sleeping surfaces are level and adjacent. The baby has their own firm, flat surface and their own bedding, but is within arm's reach for feeding and comfort. It provides proximity without the risks of sharing a duvet, pillow or soft mattress.
My parents and in-laws expect the baby to sleep in our bed. How do we handle that?

You are allowed to make a different choice from the previous generation. Be specific rather than critical: explain what you are doing (room-sharing with a bedside cot) and why you find it works for your family, without framing it as a verdict on how older relatives raised their children. Offering a concrete alternative, such as a grandparent settling the baby in their own room during daytime naps, often satisfies the closeness that grandparents are really seeking.

d.t: Colic and unsettled evenings in newborns: why it happens and what can help
q: What is colic exactly?

Colic is defined by the rule of three: crying for more than 3 hours a day, more than 3 days a week, for more than 3 weeks, in an otherwise healthy baby. It typically peaks around week 6 and resolves by 3 to 4 months in most babies. Colic is a description of a crying pattern, not a diagnosis of a specific cause. It affects roughly 1 in 5 babies and is equally common in breastfed and formula-fed infants.
What causes colic?

The honest answer is that researchers are still not certain. Leading theories include gut microbiome immaturity (colic is associated with differences in gut bacteria), sensitivity to sensory stimulation at the end of a long day, gastrointestinal motility issues, and the normal developmental PURPLE crying period. None of these theories fully explains every case. Cow's milk protein allergy (CMPA) can cause similar crying patterns in a subset of babies, but colic and CMPA are not the same thing and CMPA typically comes with additional symptoms such as reflux, blood in the stool or a rash.
Does eliminating dairy from my diet help colicky breastfed babies?

Maternal dietary elimination has modest and inconsistent evidence. For the general colic population it is unlikely to make a significant difference. However, if your baby also has other symptoms of cow's milk protein allergy such as mucous in their stools, significant reflux, a skin rash, or blood in stools, a two to four week dairy trial under the guidance of your health visitor or GP is worth considering. Eliminating dairy without clinical reason is not recommended, as it can affect maternal nutrition.
Do colic drops help?

Simethicone drops (Infacol) have not consistently outperformed placebo in clinical trials for colic. Gripe water has similarly weak evidence. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus reuteri DSM17938 has shown some benefit in reducing crying time in breastfed babies with colic in several studies, though the effect is modest and has not been replicated consistently in formula-fed infants. Your health visitor can help you weigh up what is worth trying in your specific situation.
What actually helps in the moment during a colic episode?

Movement and sound are the most consistently effective in-the-moment strategies. Holding your baby in the colic hold (baby face-down along your forearm, tummy on your arm, head near your elbow), gentle rhythmic motion such as rocking or swaying, white noise or the sound of running water, a warm bath, or skin-to-skin contact are all reported by parents as helpful. What works varies between babies. This is also why babywearing in the evenings can be very practical: it keeps your hands free while offering the movement and closeness the baby needs.
When does colic end?

Colic typically peaks at around 6 weeks of age and resolves by 3 to 4 months. By 4 months the vast majority of babies have significantly less or no evening crying. This timeline can feel endless when you are in the middle of it, but knowing there is a natural end date is genuinely reassuring. If excessive crying continues well beyond 4 months, or if your baby also has other symptoms, speak to your health visitor or GP to rule out any underlying cause.

d.t: Colic: what it is, what helps, and when it ends
q: How is colic defined exactly?

The most widely used clinical definition is the Wessel criteria: crying or fussing for more than three hours per day, on more than three days per week, for more than three weeks, in an otherwise healthy and well-fed infant. This is sometimes called the 'rule of threes.' In practice, most clinicians use colic as a descriptive label for intense, inconsolable crying in an infant where no medical cause can be found.
Does anything actually help with colic?

No single remedy reliably works for all babies, but several approaches have the most evidence. Skin-to-skin contact, rhythmic movement (rocking, bouncing, car rides), white noise, and gentle tummy pressure can calm some babies during a colic episode. Probiotics, specifically Lactobacillus reuteri, have shown modest benefit in breastfed babies in some trials. Simethicone (infant gas drops) has not shown consistent benefit in controlled trials but is considered safe to try. Eliminating cow's milk protein from the diet may help in a subset of babies where an underlying sensitivity is present.
When does colic usually end?

For the majority of babies, colic improves significantly between 3 and 4 months of age. Most cases have resolved entirely by 5 months. The peak of colic crying is typically around 6 to 8 weeks of age. This timeline is consistent across many studies and is one of the few things about colic that clinicians agree on.
How do I cope with colic as a parent?

Coping strategies matter enormously. Tag-team with a partner so neither person is the sole soother for extended periods. Accept that you cannot always stop the crying: your calm presence is valuable even when nothing is working. Use safe put-down breaks: placing the baby in a safe place and stepping away for a few minutes is far safer than caring for a baby while severely stressed. Reach out to your health visitor, GP, or a support line such as the National Childbirth Trust (NCT) helpline. Remind yourself and your partner that this is temporary and will end.

d.t: Combination feeding: mixing breastfeeding and bottle feeding
q: Why would I want to express breast milk?

There are several reasons parents choose to express: being apart from their baby (such as returning to work or a baby in special care), dealing with breast engorgement, a baby who struggles to latch, wanting a partner to help with feeding, or wanting to maintain or boost milk supply.
How long can expressed breast milk be stored in the fridge?

Expressed breast milk can be kept in the fridge for up to 8 days at 4°C or lower. If you are unsure whether your fridge reaches that temperature, or if it is slightly warmer, use the milk within 3 days.
Can I freeze expressed breast milk?

Yes. Expressed breast milk can be stored in a freezer at -18°C or lower for up to 6 months. In the ice compartment of a fridge-freezer it keeps for up to 2 weeks. Always label and date it before freezing, and store in small amounts to reduce waste.
How should I warm expressed breast milk?

You can offer it cold straight from the fridge if your baby is willing. To warm it, place the bottle in a jug of warm water or hold it under warm running water. Do not use a microwave, as microwaves can create hot spots that may burn your baby's mouth.
What should I do if I find expressing difficult?

Speak to your midwife, health visitor or a breastfeeding supporter. You can also call the National Breastfeeding Helpline 24 hours a day on 0300 100 0212. Support is available and most difficulties can be resolved with the right guidance.

d.t: Common questions parents have about baby vaccines answered
q: Are vaccines safe for babies?

Yes. Every vaccine used in the UK goes through years of rigorous safety testing before it is approved. After approval, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) continues to monitor each vaccine to make sure it remains both safe and effective.
How do vaccines work?

Vaccines teach your baby's immune system to produce antibodies against a specific disease. Because the immune system learns through the vaccine rather than through catching the real illness, the learning process is much safer than natural infection and can provide lifelong protection.
Can too many vaccines at once overwhelm my baby's immune system?

No. According to NHS guidance, receiving several vaccines at the same appointment does not overload or weaken a baby's immune system. The schedule is designed so that multiple vaccines can safely be given together.
What side effects are normal after a vaccine?

Mild reactions are common and short-lived. These include a red, swollen or sore patch at the injection site lasting around two to three days, and a mild fever or feeling unwell for one to two days. Your baby may also be upset immediately after the injection, which is completely normal.
Why does it matter if other children are vaccinated too?

When enough people in a community are vaccinated, diseases cannot spread easily, which protects those who cannot receive vaccines themselves, such as very young babies or people with certain health conditions. For measles, for example, NHS guidance indicates that around 95% vaccination coverage is needed to stop the virus circulating.

d.t: Congee as a baby first food
q: Is congee a good first food for babies?

Yes, congee is a well-established first food with a centuries-long tradition in Chinese, Japanese, Korean and other Asian cultures. It is soft, smooth and easy to swallow, and its mild flavour is well tolerated by young babies. However, plain white rice congee is low in iron and protein, so it should be enriched with ingredients such as pureed fish, chicken, egg yolk or tofu from the start. The WHO recommends that iron-rich foods be a priority from 6 months, especially for breastfed babies.
Can I add soy sauce to baby congee?

No. Soy sauce, oyster sauce and other condiments are high in salt and should not be added to food for babies under 12 months. Baby kidneys cannot process high levels of sodium effectively. Congee for babies should be prepared without any salt or seasoning sauces. The same applies to stock unless it is specifically salt-free.
How do I make congee for a 6-month-old?

Use a ratio of 1 part white rice to 10 parts water. Simmer on a low heat for 45 to 60 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the rice has broken down into a thick, smooth porridge. For a faster result, cook in a pressure cooker for around 20 minutes. Blend or pass through a sieve to achieve a very smooth texture for a 6-month-old. Stir in a pureed or finely minced iron-rich ingredient such as fish, chicken or egg yolk before serving. Do not add salt or any condiments.
Why does my baby need more than just congee?

Plain white rice congee provides carbohydrates and is easy to digest, but it is low in iron and protein. The WHO highlights iron-rich foods as a nutritional priority from 6 months, particularly for breastfed babies, because breast milk is low in iron and babies' birth stores begin to decline around this age. A diet of plain congee alone would not meet these needs. Adding pureed meat, fish, egg yolk, tofu or legumes addresses this gap and makes congee a nutritionally balanced meal.
What is the difference between congee and rice cereal?

Congee is whole rice grains cooked with a large volume of water until they break down into a soft porridge. It is a whole food prepared at home from rice and water. Commercial infant rice cereal is processed, dried and often fortified with added iron and other nutrients. Both can be part of a varied weaning diet, but homemade congee requires deliberate enrichment to match the iron content of many fortified cereals.

d.t: Constipation in babies: causes, signs and what helps
q: How do I know if my baby is constipated?

Signs to look out for include doing fewer than 3 poos in a week, passing stools that are large, hard, or pellet-like, straining or seeming in pain when trying to poo, a stomach ache that eases after a bowel movement, and a reduced appetite.
What can I do at home to help a constipated baby?

For breastfed babies who have not yet started solids, offering more frequent breastfeeds can help. For formula-fed babies, you can offer cooled boiled water between feeds. Once your baby is eating solids, a varied diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables can help keep things moving.
When should I take my baby to a GP about constipation?
The NHS advises seeing a GP if you think your baby may be constipated. Getting help early matters because the longer constipation goes on, the harder it can be to get bowel movements back to normal.
Can constipation in babies cause other problems?

Yes. If constipation continues, a cycle can develop where the baby avoids going to avoid discomfort, which makes things worse. In some cases hard stools can cause small tears that lead to bleeding. A GP can advise on appropriate treatment.
How long does treatment for constipation take to work?
According to NHS guidance, treatment may take several months to work in some cases. It is important to keep going with the recommended approach and to follow up with a GP if things are not improving.

d.t: Contact naps vs crib naps: benefits, drawbacks and how to transition
q: Are contact naps bad for babies?

No. Contact naps are biologically normal and well suited to the early months. Baby sleep research does not support the idea that being held to sleep creates long-term problems. Contact napping through the first year is a valid, responsive choice.
Is it safe to let my baby sleep on me?

Yes, with one important condition: the caregiver holding the baby must be awake and alert. Contact napping on a bed or firm sofa cushion while you are sitting up and aware is safe. Falling asleep together on a sofa or armchair is not safe and should be avoided.
When should I start putting my baby down for naps?

There is no fixed age. Attempting crib naps before around three to four months is often frustrating because sleep physiology is not mature enough to support easy independent settling. Many families begin experimenting with crib naps from around four to six months, though plenty of babies do not nap in a crib until later in the first year.
How do I transition my baby from contact naps to the crib?

The most widely recommended approach is to put your baby down while drowsy but still awake, rather than waiting for deep sleep. Warming the crib mattress briefly with a hot water bottle and removing it before you put your baby down, or placing a worn item of your clothing nearby for your scent, can also help. Expect the process to take several weeks and some repetition.
My baby will only sleep on me. Is something wrong?

Nothing is wrong. Many babies sleep exclusively on a caregiver for the first several months. It reflects how young babies are built, not a problem with you or with your baby. If you need hands-free time, a well-fitting sling can keep your baby close while freeing up your arms.
Will contact napping make it harder for my baby to sleep independently later?

The evidence does not support this concern. Research from James McKenna's Mother-Baby Behavioral Sleep Laboratory at Notre Dame and from the broader sleep science literature does not show that responding warmly to a baby's sleep needs in infancy prevents them from learning to sleep independently as they grow.

d.t: Cow's milk for babies: when it is safe and how to use it
q: When can babies drink cow's milk?

Cow's milk can be used in cooking and mixed with food from 6 months. However, the NHS advises that cow's milk should not replace breast milk or infant formula as the main drink until 12 months. After 12 months, full-fat cow's milk can become the main milk drink. Semi-skimmed milk can be introduced from 2 years once a child is eating a varied diet.
Why can't babies under 12 months have cow's milk as a main drink?

Cow's milk does not contain enough iron and other nutrients in the right proportions to meet a young baby's needs, and it contains too much protein and salt. Breast milk and infant formula are nutritionally complete for a baby under 12 months. Using dairy in cooking or mixed into food from 6 months is safe because the amounts are small.
What type of cow's milk should I give after 12 months?

Full-fat (whole) cow's milk from 12 months. Babies and toddlers need the fat and calories in full-fat milk for growth and brain development. Semi-skimmed milk can be introduced from 2 years. Skimmed milk is not recommended for children under 5.
Can I use cow's milk in porridge or baby food before 12 months?

Yes. The NHS confirms that cow's milk can be used freely in cooking from 6 months onward. This includes mixing it into porridge, mashed potato, sauces, scrambled eggs and other foods. The distinction is between using dairy in food (fine from 6 months) and offering it as a drink in a cup or bottle instead of breast or formula milk (not until 12 months).

d.t: Cradle cap: what it is, how long it lasts and how to treat it
q: What does cradle cap look like?

Cradle cap appears as patches of greasy, scaly skin on a baby's scalp and face. The scales are white or yellow and crusty, and they may flake off. The skin underneath can look pink or red on lighter skin tones, or lighter or darker on darker skin tones.
How long does cradle cap last?
Cradle cap usually clears up on its own within a few months. It is a harmless condition and does not cause your baby any discomfort.
Can I treat cradle cap at home?

Yes. You can massage an emollient or coconut oil gently into the affected area to loosen the scales, then use a soft brush to lift them before washing the scalp with a mild baby shampoo. Regular bathing with water and an emollient instead of soap also helps.
Is cradle cap contagious?
No. Cradle cap cannot spread from one baby to another. The cause is not fully understood, but it is not related to poor hygiene or infection.
When should I see a doctor about cradle cap?

See your GP if the condition does not improve after a few weeks of home care, if it spreads to cover most of the body, if the crusts bleed or leak fluid, or if the affected skin looks swollen. These signs could point to an infection or another skin condition.

d.t: Crawling milestones: when babies crawl, the different styles and what to do if they skip it
q: At what age do babies start to crawl?

Most babies start to crawl somewhere between seven and ten months, though the range is wide. Some babies are on the move as early as six months, and others do not crawl until closer to twelve months or later. A small number skip crawling altogether and go straight to walking, which is also completely normal.
Is bum shuffling instead of crawling normal?

Yes. Bum shuffling is a very common alternative to hands-and-knees crawling. Babies who shuffle on their bottoms are simply choosing a different, equally valid form of locomotion. Bum shufflers often walk a little later than crawlers, usually by around 18 months, but this is not a cause for concern.
What if my baby skips crawling altogether?

Skipping crawling entirely and going straight to pulling up and walking is a recognised, normal developmental path. Research has not shown any link between skipping crawling and later problems with learning or development. If your baby is walking independently by 18 months, there is nothing to worry about.
How does tummy time help with crawling?

Tummy time builds the shoulder, arm, and core strength that hands-and-knees crawling requires. Babies who spend regular time on their fronts while awake and supervised develop the muscle groups they will use to lift themselves up and move forward. Short, frequent sessions are more effective than occasional long ones.
When should I be concerned that my baby is not crawling?

Not crawling on its own is not a concern, especially if your baby is moving around in other ways. If your baby is not showing any independent mobility at all, such as rolling, shuffling, or scooting, by nine to ten months, it is worth mentioning to your health visitor. Always follow your doctor's or health visitor's guidance.
Do babies need special flooring or mats to learn to crawl?

No special flooring is needed. A clean, firm, flat surface such as a carpet or a foam play mat is ideal. The surface should be firm enough for your baby to push against. Very soft surfaces like deep-pile rugs or thick cushions can make it harder for a baby to generate the push they need.

d.t: C-section vs vaginal birth recovery: what's different and what's the same
q: How long is recovery from a c-section vs vaginal birth?

Hospital stay after a vaginal birth is typically 6 to 24 hours if there are no complications. After a c-section, most people stay 2 to 4 days. Full recovery at home takes longer after a c-section: most people need around 6 weeks before they feel back to normal, compared to a shorter period for uncomplicated vaginal births, though this varies a great deal depending on any tearing or stitches involved.
Can I drive after a c-section?

Most healthcare providers advise waiting around 6 weeks before driving after a c-section. You need to be confident that you can perform an emergency stop without hesitation and that you are not relying on pain relief that could affect your reactions. Always check with your GP or midwife before getting behind the wheel, and contact your car insurance provider as some policies include post-surgery conditions.
Is bleeding the same after c-section and vaginal birth?

Yes. Lochia, the postnatal bleeding and discharge from the uterus, happens after both c-section and vaginal birth. It is not related to the type of birth you had. Lochia typically lasts for up to 6 weeks and moves through three phases: bright red in the first few days, then pinkish or brownish, then yellowish-white. Contact your midwife or GP if bleeding suddenly becomes heavier, smells unpleasant, or you feel unwell alongside it.
What's the best breastfeeding position after a c-section?

Many people find the rugby hold (also called the football hold) works well after a c-section because it keeps the baby's body to your side and away from the abdominal wound, rather than resting across your stomach. Lying on your side to feed is another option that takes pressure off the incision. A breastfeeding pillow or rolled blanket can help you find a position that is comfortable for you.
When can I exercise after a c-section?

Gentle walking is encouraged from the early days after a c-section. Most healthcare providers advise waiting until your 6-week postnatal check before returning to more strenuous exercise, and some people need longer depending on how their wound is healing. Avoid lifting anything heavier than your baby for the first 6 weeks. Pelvic floor exercises can be started as soon as you feel able, even in the first days after surgery.

d.t: Cutting baby nails safely: a step-by-step guide
q: When should I start cutting my newborn's nails?

Some babies arrive with nails that are already long enough to scratch their own skin, so you may need to trim them from the very first days. Check the length regularly and trim whenever they seem sharp or jagged.
What is the safest tool for cutting a newborn's nails?
The NHS recommends using special baby nail clippers or small, round-ended safety scissors rather than adult versions. A fine emery board is another option if you prefer not to cut at all.
When is the best time to trim my baby's nails?
The easiest moment is when your baby is asleep or in a calm, relaxed state. Movement is the main cause of accidental nicks, so a sleeping baby makes the job much simpler.
Can I use an emery board instead of scissors or clippers?
Yes. Gently filing the nails with a soft emery board is a perfectly valid approach recommended by the NHS, and many parents find it feels less daunting than cutting.
What should I do if I accidentally cut my baby's finger?

Apply gentle pressure with a clean piece of cotton wool or a soft cloth until the bleeding stops. Do not use a plaster on a young baby as it can come loose and become a choking hazard. If you are concerned, contact your midwife, health visitor or GP.

d.t: Dairy for babies: cheese, yogurt and fromage frais explained
q: When can babies eat cheese?

Cheese can be introduced from 6 months as part of weaning. Full-fat pasteurised cheese is safe. Hard cheeses such as mild cheddar are popular first choices as they are easy to grate or cut into small pieces. Soft mould-ripened cheeses (brie, camembert, blue cheese) should be avoided under 12 months because of the risk of listeria. Avoid adding extra salt when cooking with cheese as it is naturally salty.
When can babies eat yogurt?

Full-fat natural or plain yogurt can be given from 6 months. It is a good source of protein, calcium and fat. Choose full-fat rather than low-fat as babies need the calories. Avoid flavoured yogurts high in added sugar. Plain natural yogurt or Greek yogurt with fresh fruit mashed in is a good alternative to sweetened products. Check the label: look for yogurts with no added sugar or sweeteners.
What is fromage frais and is it suitable for babies?

Fromage frais is a soft, creamy dairy product that is popular for babies and young children. Full-fat fromage frais is suitable from 6 months. As with yogurt, choose natural or plain varieties and add your own fruit rather than buying flavoured products, which are often high in sugar. Many fromage frais products marketed for babies and young children are lower in fat than plain fromage frais, so check the label.
Does dairy count as a milk feed for a baby under 12 months?

No. Dairy foods (cheese, yogurt, fromage frais) are solid foods, not a milk feed. They are safe and nutritious from 6 months as part of weaning, but they do not replace breast milk or infant formula as the main milk drink before 12 months. Cow's milk itself should not be the main drink until after 12 months, though dairy foods are fine from 6 months.

d.t: Introducing dairy to your baby: yoghurt, cheese and the 12-month milk rule
q: Can I give my baby yoghurt before 12 months?

Yes. Full-fat plain yoghurt can be offered as a weaning food from 6 months. The 12-month rule applies only to cows milk as a main drink replacing breast milk or formula. Dairy products used as food, including yoghurt and cheese, are appropriate from the start of weaning and are an excellent source of calcium, protein, and fat for growing babies.
Why can't babies have cows milk as a main drink before 12 months?

Cows milk has a very different nutritional profile from breast milk or formula. It contains too much protein and mineral salts, which places a burden on a young baby's kidneys. It also lacks enough iron, vitamin E, and essential fatty acids for an infant's needs, and drinking large amounts can displace iron-rich foods and contribute to iron deficiency anaemia. From 12 months, the baby's kidneys are more mature and their nutritional needs have changed sufficiently that full-fat cows milk works well as a main drink.
How much dairy does a baby or toddler need each day?

Guidance from the NHS suggests approximately 350 to 400ml of milk or its dairy equivalent per day for babies aged 6 to 12 months (including breast milk and formula). For toddlers over 12 months, around 300ml of full-fat cows milk or equivalent dairy portions per day is appropriate. Equivalent dairy includes two to three portions of yoghurt or cheese across the day.
What is the difference between CMPA and lactose intolerance?

Cows milk protein allergy (CMPA) is an immune reaction to the proteins in cows milk (casein and whey). It can cause symptoms including rashes, eczema, vomiting, diarrhoea, blood in nappies, and in severe cases anaphylaxis. Lactose intolerance is an inability to digest lactose, the sugar in milk, due to insufficient lactase enzyme. Primary lactose intolerance is rare in babies; secondary lactose intolerance can occur temporarily after a gut infection. CMPA is managed with strict dairy avoidance, while true lactose intolerance is managed differently.
Can a baby outgrow CMPA?

Most babies with IgE-mediated CMPA (the immediate allergic response type) outgrow it by 3 to 5 years of age. Most babies with non-IgE CMPA (the delayed response type) outgrow it even earlier, often by 12 months. Reintroduction of dairy is done according to a structured protocol, often called the milk ladder, under the guidance of a doctor or dietitian.
Should I give full-fat or low-fat dairy to my baby?

Always full-fat for babies and children under 2. Babies have high energy needs relative to their size, and fat is an essential source of that energy. Low-fat dairy products are not appropriate for under-2s. From 2 years, if growth and development are progressing well, semi-skimmed milk can be introduced. Skimmed milk is not appropriate for children under 5.

d.t: Dakko himo: traditional babywearing and what it offers
q: What are the TICKS rules for babywearing?

TICKS stands for five key safety checks: Tight (the carrier should be snug with no slack for baby to slump), In view at all times (you should always be able to see your baby's face by glancing down), Close enough to kiss (baby's head should be close enough that you can kiss the top without straining), Keep chin off chest (baby's airway must stay open - at least a finger-width of space under the chin), and Supported back (baby's back should be in a natural curved position with continuous support).
Is the dakko himo safe for newborns?

A dakko himo can be used from birth when it is correctly fitted and all TICKS safety rules are followed. Newborns must always be carried in the face-in position with head fully supported. If your baby was born prematurely, has a low birth weight, or has any respiratory or muscle-tone concerns, speak with your midwife, health visitor or paediatrician before using any baby carrier.
What is the M-position in babywearing?

The M-position describes the way a baby's legs should look when carried in a well-fitted carrier: knees higher than the bottom, legs spread in a natural frog or spread-squat position, with the thighs fully supported from knee to knee. This posture encourages healthy hip socket development. The International Hip Dysplasia Institute recommends this position as hip-healthy babywearing practice.
How long can I carry my baby in a dakko himo?

There is no fixed time limit. Carry for as long as both you and your baby are comfortable. Take regular breaks to check your baby's position, ensure the chin is off the chest, and confirm the airway is clear. If your back or shoulders feel strained, take a rest. Many caregivers carry for short stretches of 20 to 40 minutes and build up gradually as they grow more confident with the fit.

d.t: Daycare and sick days: what policies mean for your family
q: When does daycare require a child to stay home?

Most daycare centers follow AAP and CDC guidance, which recommends exclusion for fever above 101 F (38.3 C), uncontrolled diarrhea, vomiting twice or more in 24 hours, a rash with fever, eye discharge consistent with pink eye, and diagnosed contagious illnesses such as strep throat or hand-foot-and-mouth disease. Policies vary by center, so always read your specific enrollment agreement.
What does the '24 hours fever-free' rule mean?

Most centers require a child to be fever-free for at least 24 hours without the use of fever-reducing medication such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen before returning. This means if your child's fever breaks Monday evening only because of medication, they cannot return until Wednesday at the earliest if the fever stays away on its own through Tuesday.
Can my baby go to daycare with a runny nose?

A clear or light-colored runny nose alone, without fever or other symptoms, is generally not a reason for exclusion under AAP and CDC guidelines. Young babies get six to ten colds per year on average, and excluding for every runny nose would make attendance nearly impossible. However, always defer to your specific daycare's written policy.
How can I build a backup care plan for sick days?

Start by identifying at least two backup options before your baby starts daycare: a grandparent or trusted family member, a neighbor or close friend, a backup nanny agency in your area, or a sick-child drop-in center. Talk to your employer in advance about remote-work options and review your sick-leave policy so you are not problem-solving in a panic on the morning your baby has a fever.

d.t: Developmental play for babies aged seven to nine months: activities that actually help
q: What should a seven-month-old baby be doing during play?

At seven months, most babies are actively reaching for and grasping objects, transferring items from hand to hand, and beginning to show interest in cause and effect. During play they will often drop objects deliberately to watch them fall, mouth everything they pick up, and respond to your face and voice with smiles and babbling. There is a wide range of what is typical at this age, so follow your baby's lead rather than comparing to a checklist.
What are the best toys for babies aged seven to nine months?

The most developmentally useful toys at this age are simple ones: stacking rings, soft balls, containers with lids, small board books, and everyday household objects that are safe to mouth (like a silicone cup or a wooden spoon). Babies this age do not need electronic toys or screen-based products. Your face, your voice, and your presence are far more stimulating than any purchased toy.
What is a treasure basket and how do I set one up?

A treasure basket is a low container filled with everyday objects of varied textures, weights, and shapes. Good items include a wooden spoon, a small cardboard box, a silicone cup, a folded piece of fabric, a small smooth stone (too large to swallow), and a metal spoon. Every item must pass the mouthing test: nothing smaller than a toilet roll tube, nothing with sharp edges, nothing that could break off in small pieces. Sit nearby while your baby explores and let them choose what to investigate.
How long should play sessions be at this age?

There is no set duration. Play sessions are naturally short at seven to nine months because babies have limited sustained attention. A few minutes of focused interaction is completely normal and healthy. The most important thing is that you follow your baby's cues: when they look away, fuss, or seem tired, the session is over. Several short sessions spread through the day are more effective than one long one.
Is screen time okay for babies at seven to nine months?

The AAP advises avoiding screen-based media for babies under 18 to 24 months, with the exception of video calls. Screens do not provide the back-and-forth interaction that develops language and attachment, and the sensory input they offer is narrow compared to handling real objects, being outside, or interacting with a caregiver. Everyday life is far richer for brain development than any screen.
How do I encourage my baby to babble more?

The single most effective thing you can do is respond to every sound your baby makes. When they babble, look at them, smile, and make a sound back. This back-and-forth, often called serve and return, tells your baby that communication works. Narrating what you are doing throughout the day also provides a steady stream of language input. Songs with gaps where your baby can 'fill in' sounds are especially effective.

d.t: The dream feed: what it is, how to do it and whether it actually works
q: What is a dream feed?

A dream feed is a feeding given to a drowsy or lightly sleeping baby, typically between 10pm and 11pm, before the parents go to bed. The idea is to top up the baby's milk intake without fully waking them, extending the first stretch of sleep and giving the parents a longer uninterrupted window before the next waking. The baby is never fully roused; instead they feed in a semi-conscious state.
Does the dream feed actually work?

It works well for some babies and not at all for others. Research and clinical experience both support the idea that topping up a baby's milk intake at the start of the night can extend the first stretch of sleep, particularly in the early months. However, the effect varies considerably. Some babies wake at the same time regardless; others extend their first stretch significantly. It is worth trying consistently for a week or two before deciding whether it is helping for your baby.
How do I do a dream feed without waking my baby?

Lift your baby slowly and carefully, supporting their head, and offer the breast or bottle without turning on bright lights or making much noise. Most babies will root and latch or accept the teat without waking fully. After the feed, keep them upright briefly for a gentle wind, then transfer them back to their sleep surface. Move slowly throughout. The whole process should be calm and quiet.
When should I stop doing the dream feed?

Most parents find the dream feed stops being useful somewhere between four and six months. As babies mature and begin to consolidate their longest sleep stretch into the early part of the night independently, the dream feed can actually start disrupting their natural sleep pattern rather than extending it. If your baby is regularly waking shortly after the dream feed, or if the dream feed no longer seems to extend the first stretch, it is probably time to drop it. Wean it gradually over one to two weeks if you prefer.
Can I dream feed a breastfed baby?

Yes. Many breastfeeding parents find the dream feed works well. The baby latches and feeds in a drowsy state, and because they are not fully awake the feed tends to be shorter than a fully awake night feed. Some parents worry that a dream feed will affect supply or confuse the feeding relationship, but this is generally not a concern with an established feeder.
Is the dream feed the same as a night feed?

Not exactly. A night feed happens when a baby wakes and signals hunger; the feed is offered in response. A dream feed is initiated by the parent at a set time while the baby is still asleep. The main difference is who decides when the feed happens. A dream feed is a proactive strategy to consolidate early sleep; a responsive night feed is a reaction to hunger cues.

d.t: Drinks and cups for babies: water, milk and moving off bottles
q: When can I give my baby water?

The NHS advises waiting until your baby is around 6 months old before offering water. Before that age, breast milk or first infant formula provides all the fluid your baby needs. When you start introducing solid foods at around 6 months, you can offer small sips of cooled boiled tap water alongside meals in a cup. There is no need to offer water before solids begin.
Can babies drink cow's milk before 12 months?

Cow's milk should not be given as your baby's main drink before 12 months of age. It does not contain enough iron and other nutrients to meet a young baby's needs, and it can put strain on developing kidneys. However, cow's milk is fine to use in cooking or mixed into solid foods from around 6 months. After 12 months, whole cow's milk can become your child's main milk drink.
What type of cup is best for a baby?

The NHS recommends introducing an open cup or a free-flow cup without a valve from around 6 months. These cup types help babies learn a genuine sipping action, which supports healthy teeth and speech development. Cups with a non-spill valve, sometimes called sippy cups, are not recommended by the NHS because they require the same sucking action as a bottle and do not help your baby make progress toward independent drinking.
When should I stop bottle feeding?

The NHS recommends moving babies off bottles and onto cups by around 12 months of age. Using bottles beyond this age is linked to tooth decay and can affect speech development. Starting a cup from around 6 months makes the eventual transition much gentler. If your baby is resistant, try replacing one bottle feed at a time with a cup, starting with daytime feeds and leaving the bedtime feed until last.

d.t: Dropping to one nap: when babies are ready and how to make the transition smoother
q: When do most babies drop from two naps to one?

Most babies make the transition somewhere between 13 and 18 months, though some manage it as early as 12 months. The range is wide, and there is no single right age. Following your baby's readiness cues matters far more than the number on the calendar.
How do I know if my baby is ready to drop a nap?

The clearest sign is consistently resisting the second nap for two or more weeks running, not just on occasional days. Other signs include taking a very long time to fall asleep at the second nap and the second nap pushing bedtime so late that nights become harder. One or two difficult days is not enough to signal readiness, especially during a developmental leap or illness.
What time should the one nap be?

Aiming for a nap that starts around 12 to 1pm works well for most babies once the transition is settled. Starting the single nap too early, say at 10am, often means the baby is overtired again by late afternoon and struggles to reach bedtime without a meltdown. Shifting the nap later gradually, by about 15 to 30 minutes every few days, is a gentler approach than moving it all at once.
What do I do during the transition period when they seem to need both naps some days?

A flexible approach tends to work best during the two-to-six weeks the transition usually takes. On days when tiredness is obvious and one nap clearly is not enough, a short catnap in the pushchair or car in the late afternoon can prevent overtiredness without fully resetting back to two naps. An early bedtime on days when the nap is short or skipped is also genuinely helpful.
Will dropping a nap affect night sleep?

For most babies, night sleep stays the same or actually improves once they have settled into one nap. Total daytime sleep drops from around three hours across two naps to roughly two to two-and-a-half hours in one nap, but overnight sleep generally holds steady. If nights become more disrupted during the transition, bringing bedtime forward can help prevent overtiredness from building up.
What if my toddler fights the single nap too?

It is common for the single nap to be short or inconsistent for the first few weeks after the transition. Capping the nap at no more than around two hours is generally a good idea to protect night sleep. If your toddler consistently naps for less than 45 minutes and this does not improve after a few weeks, it is worth talking to your health visitor or a sleep consultant, who can help you look at the full picture of their sleep.
My baby is under 12 months and fighting the second nap. Should I drop it?

Babies under 12 months almost always still need two naps, even if they resist one of them on some days. Resistance during a developmental leap, a bout of illness, or a disrupted week is not the same as readiness. Dropping the second nap too early typically leads to overtiredness and more difficult nights rather than better sleep.

d.t: Dummies and pacifiers: benefits, risks, and when to stop
q: Do dummies reduce the risk of SIDS?

Yes. Multiple studies have found that offering a dummy at the start of sleep is associated with a reduced risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). The mechanism is not fully understood, but current evidence is strong enough that organisations like the American Academy of Pediatrics include dummy use in their safe sleep guidance.
Will a dummy affect my ability to breastfeed?

The evidence on this is mixed. Some studies suggest early dummy use may be linked to shorter breastfeeding duration, while others find no effect. The widely accepted practical advice is to wait until breastfeeding is well established, usually around three to four weeks, before introducing a dummy. This reduces the chance of interfering with latch and milk supply in the early weeks.
When should I stop using a dummy?

Most health organisations recommend weaning off the dummy by around 12 months, and ideally before 18 months, to reduce the risk of dental effects and ear infections. By age three, continued use is associated with a higher risk of changes in tooth and jaw alignment, so stopping well before that age is the general advice.
Is it safe to dip a dummy in honey or sugar to help my baby accept it?

No. You should never dip a dummy in honey, sugar, or any sweet substance. Honey is not safe for babies under 12 months due to the risk of infant botulism. Sugar on a dummy raises the risk of tooth decay and can contribute to a preference for sweet tastes. Always offer a clean, dry dummy.

d.t: Dummies and pacifiers: pros, cons and safe use
q: When is the right time to introduce a dummy?

If you are breastfeeding, it is generally recommended to wait until feeding is well established before introducing a dummy. This is usually around four weeks old, though the timing varies for every parent and baby. Once breastfeeding is going well, introducing a dummy should not make nursing more difficult. If a health professional advises using a dummy sooner, for example for a premature baby or one receiving CPAP ventilation, follow their guidance.
Can using a dummy lower the risk of SIDS?

Some research suggests that offering a dummy at sleep times could help reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). The NHS advises parents to think about using a dummy to settle their baby to sleep, as this may have a protective effect. The exact reason is not yet fully understood. If you use a dummy, offer it for every sleep rather than occasionally.
What should I avoid when using a dummy?

Never attach a dummy to a cord or clip around your baby's neck, as this is a strangulation hazard. Do not put anything sweet on it, including honey. Do not offer the dummy while your baby is awake and playing, only at sleep time. If the dummy falls out during sleep, there is no need to put it back in.
When should I stop using a dummy?

The Lullaby Trust recommends gently phasing out dummy use between six and twelve months. Longer-term use is linked with potential concerns such as misaligned teeth and a higher chance of ear infections.
What if my baby refuses a dummy?

Not every baby will accept a dummy, and that is perfectly fine. Never force a baby to take one. Following other safer sleep practices, such as placing your baby on their back to sleep in their own sleep space in a smoke-free environment, provides a strong layer of protection against SIDS even without a dummy.

d.t: Early childhood education and care: what research says about the first years
q: What are the most important things I can do to support my baby's brain development in the first year?

The most impactful things are responsive, consistent caregiving: talking, singing, reading aloud, and making eye contact during everyday routines. Serve-and-return interactions, where you respond to your baby's coos, gestures, and expressions, build neural connections faster than any toy or screen. Keeping stress low and ensuring your baby feels secure also matters enormously, because the stress-response system is shaped heavily in the first year.
Is nursery care harmful for babies under one year old?

High-quality nursery care is not harmful. The key variables are quality, not setting: warm and responsive caregivers, low child-to-staff ratios, and a predictable routine matter far more than whether care happens at home or in a nursery. Research from the NICHD Study of Early Child Care found that quality of care, whether at home or in a centre, was the strongest predictor of developmental outcomes.
When does the sensitive period for language development end?

The brain is most plastic for language acquisition from birth through about age 7, with the sharpest sensitivity in the first three years. Babies begin distinguishing the sounds of their home language as early as 6 months and start losing the ability to distinguish non-native phonemes around 10 to 12 months. This does not mean language learning stops after age 3, but the ease and depth of acquisition are greatest in the early years.
How much screen time is appropriate for toddlers under two?

The WHO recommends no screen time at all for children under 1 year, and no more than one hour per day of high-quality programming for children aged 3 to 4. For children aged 1 to 2, the WHO advises avoiding sedentary screen time. The American Academy of Pediatrics allows video calls (because they are interactive and social) but discourages passive viewing for children under 18 months. The concern is not screens themselves but the displacement of serve-and-return interaction, movement, and sleep.

d.t: Early morning wake-ups: why your baby wakes at 5am and how to push it later
q: Why does my baby always wake at 5am?

The early morning hours between 4am and 6am are when sleep is naturally at its lightest. Cortisol (the wake hormone) begins rising from around 4am, and the melatonin that has been sustaining overnight sleep starts to fall. This means your baby is cycling through lighter sleep just as dawn breaks and household sounds begin. Any small trigger, a noise, a shaft of light, a brief hunger cue, is more likely to cause full waking at this time than earlier in the night.
Will putting my baby to bed later fix the 5am wake?

Usually no, and it often makes things worse. A baby who goes to bed later is more likely to be overtired, which can actually worsen early morning waking by increasing fragmented sleep in the second half of the night. Counter-intuitively, an earlier bedtime often helps more than a later one, particularly if your baby is accumulating sleep debt from short naps or early starts. The relationship between bedtime and morning wake time is not as simple as later in, later out.
Do blackout blinds really help with early waking?

Yes, they are often one of the most effective single changes for early morning waking. Light is one of the most powerful cues to the circadian rhythm, and even modest light coming in from around curtain edges can be enough to trigger full waking in a baby who is already in a light sleep phase at dawn. Proper blackout (where you cannot see your hand in front of your face) makes a genuine difference for many families, particularly in summer.
Could my baby's nap schedule be causing the 5am wake?

Yes. An overly long awake window before bedtime can increase sleep pressure and cause early waking, as the body burns through its sleep debt faster. Equally, too-short naps or too few naps during the day can lead to overtiredness, which produces more fragmented early morning sleep. If early waking is a consistent pattern, checking that total daytime sleep is appropriate for the age and that the wake window before bed is not too long is a good place to start.
What is the wake-to-sleep technique?

Wake-to-sleep involves gently rousing your baby very slightly about 30 to 45 minutes before they typically wake early. The idea is to nudge them into a new sleep cycle just as they would otherwise be ending one and moving into the light phase that leads to full waking. It is done very gently, just enough to see a slight stir, not to wake them fully. It has mixed results and takes a week or so of consistency to assess, but some parents find it helpful for very predictable early morning waking.
When should I accept early waking as part of my child's temperament?

If you have addressed the environment (proper blackout, appropriate temperature, no noise triggers), checked the schedule (appropriate wake windows, no overtiredness), and tried a temporarily earlier bedtime, and your child consistently wakes before 6am, it may simply be their natural rhythm. Some children, particularly those between 18 months and 3 years, are genuinely early risers. A toddler clock that shows a visual okay-to-get-up cue can help them learn to stay in their room quietly until a reasonable time even if they do wake early.

d.t: Eggs for babies: when they are safe and how to serve them
q: When can babies eat eggs?

Eggs can be introduced from 6 months as part of weaning. The NHS recommends introducing eggs (and other allergens) early, rather than delaying, to reduce the risk of egg allergy. Eggs are one of the top allergens so should be introduced early, one at a time, and the baby watched for any reaction over the following few hours.
Do eggs need to be fully cooked for babies?

For babies under 12 months, eggs should be fully cooked so both the white and yolk are solid, unless they carry the British Lion mark. Lion-marked hen eggs (the vast majority sold in UK supermarkets) have been assessed as safe to eat with a runny yolk even for young babies and pregnant women, due to vaccination of hens against salmonella. Non-Lion-marked eggs, duck, goose and quail eggs should all be fully cooked for babies.
How do I serve eggs to a baby?

Scrambled egg is a popular first option as it is soft, easy to pick up, and can be made without salt. Hard-boiled egg can be served sliced, mashed, or as egg soldiers with toast. Omelette strips also work well as a finger food. Avoid adding salt. From 6 months, eggs can also be used in cooking including pancakes, frittata and eggy bread.
What are the signs of egg allergy in babies?

Signs of egg allergy usually appear within minutes to two hours of eating egg and can include hives or a rash around the mouth and face, swelling, runny or blocked nose, red watery eyes, tummy pain, vomiting or diarrhoea. Severe anaphylaxis is rare but possible. If there is any swelling of the lips or tongue, difficulty breathing, or collapse, call 999 immediately.

d.t: 8-month sleep regression: what is happening and what helps
q: Is the 8-month sleep regression a real thing?

Sleep can become more disrupted in the second half of the first year. The NHS notes that growth spurts, teething and illnesses can all affect how your baby sleeps at any stage, and that you should be prepared to change routines as your baby grows and enters different stages. A temporary change in sleep is a normal part of development, not a sign something is wrong.
How much sleep does a baby need at 6-12 months?

According to NHS guidance, babies in the 6-12 month range typically need around 15 hours of total sleep across a 24-hour period, with most of that occurring at night. Individual babies vary, and your baby's pattern may not match others of the same age.
What can I do to help my baby sleep better during this phase?

The NHS recommends a consistent, calming bedtime routine that includes activities such as a bath, changing into nightclothes, dimming the lights, reading a story or singing. Keeping the night environment quiet and low-key, and handling night feeds without stimulating play, can help your baby learn that night is for sleep.
When should I talk to a health visitor about my baby's sleep?
If sleep disruption is persistent or is significantly affecting your family, the NHS advises reaching out to your health visitor, who can offer tailored guidance for your baby's specific situation.
Does sharing a room still matter at 8 months?

NHS guidance recommends that babies sleep in the same room as a parent for at least the first 6 months. After that, the arrangement is a family decision, and your health visitor can advise if you are unsure.

d.t: 18-month sleep regression: why your toddler has stopped sleeping and what helps
q: Is the 18-month sleep regression real?

Yes. The 18-month sleep regression is a recognised and well-documented period of disrupted sleep that affects many toddlers between around 16 and 22 months. It is driven by a combination of genuine developmental changes: a rapid language explosion, a surge in independence and self-assertion, the first and sometimes second molars coming through, and a peak in separation anxiety. These are real neurological and physical events, not a parenting problem, and they temporarily disrupt sleep that had previously been settled.
Why is my 18-month-old suddenly fighting bedtime?

Bedtime battles at 18 months usually come from a combination of factors. Your toddler is asserting their independence and now has the language and understanding to actively refuse. They also know from experience that you come back when they cry, which makes them more likely to protest. Separation anxiety peaks around this age, so they genuinely do not want you to leave. On top of that, molars can cause discomfort that makes lying down uncomfortable. Keeping a consistent, predictable bedtime routine helps enormously, even when bedtime feels like a battle.
How long does the 18-month regression last?

For most toddlers the 18-month regression lasts between two and six weeks. Some children sail through in a couple of weeks with only mild disruption. For others, particularly those going through a lot of developmental change at once, it can stretch to six weeks or slightly longer. If disrupted sleep continues well beyond six to eight weeks, or your toddler seems unwell or in pain, it is worth speaking to your health visitor or GP.
Should I sleep train during the regression?

Most sleep experts suggest waiting until the regression has passed before starting or restarting formal sleep training. Trying to change sleep habits during a period of peak developmental disruption is harder for you and harder for your toddler. That said, the regression is a good time to lay the groundwork: keep the bedtime routine consistent, avoid introducing any new sleep associations you do not want to keep long term, and check that wake windows are right for your toddler's age. Once the regression lifts, those foundations make any further changes much easier.
My toddler was sleeping through and now wakes every night. Is this normal?

Yes, this is one of the most common patterns parents describe during the 18-month regression. A toddler who had been sleeping through reliably can suddenly start waking once or several times a night. This feels alarming if it comes out of nowhere, but it is a typical feature of the regression rather than a sign that something is wrong. Responding calmly and consistently, without introducing new habits you do not want to keep, is usually enough. Most toddlers return to their previous pattern within a few weeks.
When does the 18-month sleep regression end?

There is no fixed end date, but most toddlers come through the 18-month regression within two to six weeks. The clearest sign it is lifting is that your toddler starts settling at bedtime more easily again and night waking reduces without you having changed anything. If you have kept a consistent routine throughout the regression, sleep usually returns to its previous pattern fairly quickly once the developmental burst it was driven by settles down.

d.t: Elterngeld: parental leave payment explained
q: How much Elterngeld will I receive if I was earning 3,000 EUR net per month?

At 3,000 EUR net per month, the replacement rate is 65 percent, giving you approximately 1,950 EUR per month as Basiselterngeld. The maximum monthly payment is capped at 1,800 EUR, so your actual benefit would be 1,800 EUR per month. If you choose ElterngeldPlus instead, you receive half the Basiselterngeld amount, which would be 900 EUR per month, but you can receive it for double the number of months.
Can both parents receive Elterngeld at the same time?

Yes, both parents can receive Elterngeld at the same time. The total pool of months for most families is 14 months of Basiselterngeld. One parent can take a maximum of 12 months, and the additional 2 months are specifically reserved for the second parent. Both parents can draw their months concurrently, meaning they both stop working (or reduce hours) and claim simultaneously, or they can split the months consecutively. If you use ElterngeldPlus, both parents can also claim the Partnerschaftsbonus simultaneously, earning 4 extra months each when both work 25 to 30 hours per week at the same time.
What is the difference between Basiselterngeld and ElterngeldPlus?

Basiselterngeld is the standard benefit. It pays 65 to 67 percent of your average net income, between a minimum of 300 EUR and a maximum of 1,800 EUR per month, and can be taken for up to 14 months in total. ElterngeldPlus pays half the Basiselterngeld amount per month but can be received for twice as long. It is designed for parents who return to work part-time after birth. One month of Basiselterngeld equals two months of ElterngeldPlus, so the total money received is the same if you use the full allocation. The advantage of ElterngeldPlus is that it extends income support while you work reduced hours, and it enables the Partnerschaftsbonus.
How does Cubby help during parental leave?

Cubby is a free baby care app that helps parents track feeds, naps, nappy changes, and milestones in one place. During parental leave, when days blur together and both parents are often sharing care, Cubby makes it easy to log what happened and see the full picture at a glance. You can share your baby's daily logs with a partner, grandparent, or carer so everyone stays in sync without relying on memory or messages. Cubby also surfaces helpful articles and reminders so you have trusted information close at hand during the newborn weeks.

d.t: Elternzeit: how both parents can take parental leave
q: Can both parents take Elternzeit at the same time?

Yes. Both parents can take Elternzeit simultaneously. There is no requirement to take it sequentially. This is a deliberate feature of the BEEG legislation, designed to make it easier for both parents to be present together in the early months. Both parents simply each apply to their respective employer separately, giving the required seven weeks' written notice.
What is the difference between Elternzeit and Elterngeld?

Elternzeit is the legal right to take unpaid leave from work, granted by the BEEG (Bundeselterngeld- und Elternzeitgesetz). Elterngeld is a separate income-replacement benefit paid by the state during part of that leave. You can take Elternzeit without receiving Elterngeld (for example after Elterngeld months are used up), and the two are administered differently - Elternzeit is a matter between you and your employer, while Elterngeld is applied for through the Elterngeldstelle at your local Jugendamt or Familienkasse.
How much notice do I need to give my employer for Elternzeit?

The BEEG requires seven weeks' written notice before Elternzeit begins. This applies to both the first period of leave and to any changes in the planned leave schedule. The notice must be given in writing (not by email unless your employer has explicitly accepted electronic form), must clearly state the start and end dates, and must be received by the employer at least seven weeks before the leave starts.
Is my job protected during Elternzeit?

Yes. Employers are prohibited from giving notice of dismissal to an employee who has applied for or is taking Elternzeit. This protection begins from the date the application for Elternzeit is submitted (at the earliest eight weeks before the leave begins) and ends at the close of the Elternzeit period. The protection applies to both parents equally and regardless of whether they are taking leave simultaneously or sequentially.

d.t: When to seek urgent care in the UAE: numbers and danger signs
q: What number do I call in an emergency in the UAE?

Call 999 for police, ambulance, or fire across all UAE emirates. In Dubai and Abu Dhabi you can also call 998 to reach the ambulance service directly, which can be faster. Save both numbers in your phone before your baby arrives.
When should I take my baby to A&E in the UAE?

Go to A&E if your baby has a high fever (above 38°C if under 3 months, or above 39°C if 3 to 6 months), difficulty breathing, a rash with fever, persistent vomiting, signs of dehydration (sunken fontanelle, dry mouth, no wet nappies), or inconsolable crying that lasts more than 2 hours. Call 999 immediately if your baby is not breathing, has a seizure, loses consciousness, may have swallowed something poisonous, or has suffered severe burns.
What temperature counts as a fever in babies in the UAE?

A temperature of 38°C or above is considered a fever in any baby. In babies under 3 months, any fever of 38°C or higher is a reason to go to A&E immediately. In babies aged 3 to 6 months, a fever of 39°C or higher, or any fever that persists more than a day, should prompt an A&E visit or urgent call to your paediatrician.
Which hospitals have children's emergency departments in Dubai?

Latifa Hospital (government, Oud Metha) and Al Jalila Children's Specialty Hospital (government, Al Jaddaf) are the two main children's hospitals in Dubai. Most large private hospitals, including Mediclinic City Hospital, Saudi German Hospital, and American Hospital, also have paediatric A&E services. Check with your insurance provider which network hospitals are covered before an emergency arises.
Does my insurance cover A&E visits in the UAE?

Most comprehensive health insurance plans in the UAE cover A&E visits, but co-pays and network restrictions vary. Government A&E is free for UAE nationals; for expatriates, using a government facility without insurance will usually incur charges at the point of care. Private A&E is generally faster for non-life-threatening situations and is often covered by insurance if the hospital is in your network. Always carry your insurance card when visiting any hospital.

d.t: Extended family in baby care: benefits and boundaries
q: How do I tell grandparents about safe sleep guidelines if they did things differently?

Choose a calm moment outside of the immediate care situation and frame the conversation around current guidance rather than criticism. You might say something like: 'The NHS and WHO now recommend babies sleep on their backs on a firm, flat surface with no loose bedding. I know things were done differently when you were raising children, and I understand it can feel strange. This is what we are following.' Providing a short, clear source such as the NHS safe sleep page can help, because it makes clear the guidance is coming from health authorities rather than being a personal preference. Most grandparents want what is best for the baby and will adapt once they understand the reasons.
Is it harmful to let grandparents be primary caregivers while I return to work?

No. Research consistently shows that secure attachment is not limited to one caregiver. Babies can form strong, secure attachments with grandparents, childminders, and nursery workers alongside their primary parent. What matters for secure attachment is responsiveness and consistency, not exclusivity. Grandparent care has additional advantages: it is typically flexible, provided by someone who loves the child, and involves a degree of cultural and family continuity. The key is ensuring grandparents are following current safety and health guidance, especially around sleep, diet, and any medical needs specific to your baby.
What should I do when extended family members give advice I disagree with?

You can acknowledge advice without following it. A simple 'thank you, I will bear that in mind' lets you receive input without committing to it. For advice that conflicts with official guidance on safety, health, or wellbeing, it is worth explaining your position clearly and calmly: 'We have decided to follow current NHS guidance on this, which recommends a different approach.' You do not need to justify every parenting decision, but where safety is involved, being clear and consistent is more important than keeping the peace in the short term. If the same disagreement recurs, returning to a written source such as official NHS or WHO guidance can depersonalise the conversation.
How do I ask extended family for help without feeling like I am imposing?

Most family members who want to help genuinely welcome being asked. Vague offers of help ('let me know if you need anything') are hard to act on. Specific requests are much easier: 'Could you come over on Thursday morning so I can sleep?' or 'Would you be able to cook a meal we could freeze?' Research on social support shows that people who receive specific, concrete requests are more likely to follow through and feel useful than those given open-ended invitations. Accepting help is not a sign of failure. It is a recognition that raising a baby was never meant to be a one-person endeavour.

d.t: Fascia and babywearing: tradition and safety guidelines
q: What are the TICKS babywearing safety guidelines?

TICKS stands for: Tight (the carrier should be snug so the baby cannot slump); In view at all times (you should always be able to see your baby's face by looking down); Close enough to kiss (baby's head is close enough to kiss by tipping your chin down); Keep chin off chest (ensure there is a finger-width space between the baby's chin and their chest to keep the airway open); Supported back (the baby's back is supported in a natural curved position and the baby cannot lean away from the wearer). These guidelines apply to all carriers including wraps, buckle carriers, ring slings, and mei tais.
What is the M-position in babywearing?

The M-position, also called the spread-squat position or frog-leg position, describes the way a baby's legs should be positioned in a carrier to support healthy hip development. The baby's knees should be higher than their bottom, with the fabric or carrier seat supporting the thighs from knee to knee. When viewed from the front, the baby's legs form an M shape. This position is recommended by the International Hip Dysplasia Institute as optimal for hip socket development in young babies.
Can I use a fascia wrap with a newborn?

Yes. Woven wraps and stretchy wraps are among the most versatile carriers for newborns because they can be tied to support the baby in a fully upright or slightly reclined position with legs in the M-position and the head fully supported. Newborns should always be worn in a position that keeps the airway open: chin off chest, face visible, and the wrap snug enough to prevent slumping. If you are new to babywearing, a consultation with a babywearing consultant or a sling library session is strongly recommended.
When should I stop babywearing?

There is no set age at which babywearing must stop. Many families continue to use carriers for toddlers, and carriers designed for toddlers can safely carry children up to 20 kg or more. The practical limit is usually when the child consistently prefers to walk, or when the parent finds it physically uncomfortable. The AAP notes that babywearing can be continued safely as long as the weight limit of the carrier is respected and the child is positioned safely.

d.t: Feeding schedule vs demand feeding: what the evidence says
q: How many times a day should a newborn feed?

Newborns typically need 8 to 12 feeds every 24 hours, which averages roughly one feed every two to three hours. This includes night feeds. The NHS and AAP both recommend feeding in response to hunger cues rather than watching the clock, as individual babies vary considerably in how often they need to feed.
Does feeding on demand spoil a baby or create bad habits?

No. Responsive feeding does not spoil a baby or create bad habits. In the first months of life, babies cannot self-regulate or manipulate caregivers. Feeding promptly in response to hunger cues builds trust, supports brain development, and is recommended by all major health organisations including the WHO and AAP.
Will a feeding schedule reduce milk supply?

Yes, it can. Breast milk supply works on a supply-and-demand basis. The more frequently milk is removed from the breast, the more is produced. Stretching feeds by the clock reduces the number of times milk is removed each day, which can signal the body to make less. This is one of the main reasons the WHO, NHS, and AAP all recommend feeding in response to hunger cues rather than on a fixed schedule for breastfed babies.
When do babies naturally start spacing out their feeds?

Most babies begin to develop a more predictable feeding rhythm between six and eight weeks of age as their stomach capacity grows and they become more efficient at feeding. By around three months, many babies have naturally settled into a pattern of feeding every three to four hours during the day, though this varies between individuals. This pattern tends to emerge on its own without needing to impose a schedule.

d.t: Fine motor skills in babies: from palmar grasp to pincer and beyond
q: What is the palmar grasp reflex?

The palmar grasp reflex is a newborn reflex where a baby automatically curls their fingers around anything placed in their palm. It is present from birth and gradually fades between 3 and 6 months as voluntary hand control develops.
When does the pincer grasp develop?

The pincer grasp, using thumb and forefinger to pick up small objects, begins to emerge around 8 to 9 months and becomes well established by 12 months. It develops gradually from the raking grasp that comes before it.
What activities support fine motor development in babies?

Activities that support fine motor development include offering objects of different sizes and textures to grasp, nesting cups and containers to fill and empty, soft foods as finger foods, water play with pouring, and age-appropriate art activities like finger painting and clay for older babies.
What is bilateral coordination?

Bilateral coordination is the ability to use both hands together in a coordinated way. Early signs appear around 6 to 7 months when babies begin passing objects from one hand to the other. It continues developing through the toddler years.
What are signs of fine motor delay in a baby?

Signs that may be worth discussing with a health visitor include not reaching for objects by 4 to 5 months, not transferring objects hand to hand by 7 months, not using any kind of grasp to pick up objects by 9 months, or a strong preference for one hand before 18 months.
Does it matter if a baby strongly prefers one hand?

A strong hand preference before 18 months can sometimes indicate a difference in muscle tone or nerve development on one side and is worth mentioning to a health visitor. Most babies do not show a clear hand preference until 2 to 3 years of age.

d.t: Finger foods for babies: safe shapes, textures and ideas for 6 to 12 months
q: When can I start offering finger foods?

Soft finger foods can be introduced from 6 months, alongside or instead of purees, as soon as your baby shows the three signs of weaning readiness: sitting upright with minimal support, good head and neck control, and loss of the tongue-thrust reflex. At this age, babies use a raking or palmar grasp and can manage large, very soft pieces. You do not need to wait until 7 or 8 months to introduce finger foods.
How do I know if a finger food texture is safe?

Use the squish test. If you can squish the food easily between your finger and thumb with no real effort, it is appropriate for a baby under 10 months. If it resists squishing, it is too firm. Food that squishes easily in an adult's fingers will squish easily in a baby's gum, even before teeth arrive. Gums are surprisingly effective at breaking down soft food.
What is the difference between gagging and choking?

Gagging is a normal, protective reflex. The baby coughs, sputters, makes retching sounds, and may go red. They can breathe, make noise, and recover within seconds. Gagging protects the airway by pushing food forward before it is ready to be swallowed. Choking is different: the baby goes quiet or makes very little sound, cannot cough effectively, may turn blue, and is in visible distress. Choking is a blocked airway and requires immediate first aid action.
Do babies need teeth to eat finger foods?

No. Babies do not need teeth to eat soft finger foods. Gums are harder than they look and can break down soft food effectively. Many babies do not get their first teeth until 8 to 10 months or later, yet can manage soft finger foods from 6 months. Teeth do help with firmer foods, so the progression to slightly firmer textures often follows the appearance of teeth, but soft food is fully manageable without them.
Are rice cakes safe for babies?

Plain, unsalted rice cakes are often suggested as a finger food, but they dissolve into a sticky paste in the mouth rather than breaking into manageable pieces, which some babies find easier and others find more difficult. They are low in nutrition and not the most useful weaning food. If you offer them, choose unsalted varieties and offer them one at a time rather than in a large piece that could break off unexpectedly.
What foods should I avoid giving my baby as finger foods?

Avoid whole grapes, whole cherry tomatoes, whole blueberries (cut all round foods lengthways into quarters), hard raw vegetables such as raw carrot or celery, whole nuts, large seeds, popcorn, marshmallows, and large globs of nut butter. Also avoid any food with added salt or honey. Foods that break into hard shards, like some crackers, can be an issue; check how they behave in your fingers before offering them.

d.t: Your baby's first birthday: what changes, what to expect and the 12-month leap
q: What developmental changes happen around the first birthday?
