Less back-and-forth interaction slows language development and reduces the richness of the learning environment. Turning off the TV when it is not the focus helps protect that interaction time.
Can educational apps help my toddler learn?

Research reviewed by the AAP shows that children under about 2.5 years learn significantly better from a real person than from a video or app, even when the content is identical. Toddlers from around age 2 can begin to transfer learning from high-quality interactive apps, but only when a parent or caregiver watches alongside and connects what is on screen to the real world. An app used alone, without that adult bridge, is far less effective than it might appear.
What should I do if my child has already been watching a lot of screens?

Guidelines are a target, not a verdict. If your child has had more screen time than recommended, the most useful step is a gradual reset rather than a sudden stop. Introduce more physical play, outdoor time, and shared reading to fill the gaps. Talk to your health visitor, paediatrician, or family doctor if you are worried about development. They can assess your child individually and give you a plan suited to your family.

d.t: Self-care for new parents: why it matters and simple steps
q: Is it normal to feel exhausted after having a baby?

Yes. Newborns typically sleep in short stretches, waking several times through the night, which means no single block of uninterrupted sleep for parents. This is a normal part of the early weeks, not a sign that something is wrong.
When should I worry that tiredness is something more serious?

If you find yourself unable to sleep even when your baby is settled, feel persistently hopeless or down, or lose interest in things you normally enjoy, speak to your GP or health visitor. These can be signs of postnatal depression, which responds well to early treatment.
Does exercise really help when you are exhausted?
According to NHS guidance, regular exercise can help you feel less tired. A short walk with the pram is enough to count. You do not need a gym or a structured workout.
How can my partner help me get more rest?

If you are formula feeding, your partner can take one or more night feeds entirely. If you are breastfeeding, your partner can handle nappy changes and the morning routine so you can sleep a little longer after a feed. Once breastfeeding is established, a bottle of expressed milk for one night feed is another option.
What if I have no partner or family nearby?

You can still ask friends to visit with the specific purpose of watching the baby while you rest. Organisations such as Home-Start offer volunteer home visitors who can provide practical support. Your health visitor can also point you towards local services.

d.t: Baby self-feeding: when to start, what to offer and how to encourage it
q: When can babies start to self-feed?

Babies can be offered soft finger foods from 6 months, alongside or instead of purees. At 6 months, they use a raking or palmar grasp to hold large, soft pieces. By 9 to 12 months, the more precise pincer grasp develops, allowing babies to pick up smaller pieces. You can introduce self-feeding at whatever stage you start solids, adjusting the size and texture of food to match your baby's current grip ability.
What finger food shapes are safest?

The safest shape for babies under 12 months is a long stick or strip about the length and width of an adult finger. This lets a baby hold the food in their fist with a portion sticking out, making it easy to bite without the piece ending up deep in the mouth. Round or coin-shaped foods are the highest choking risk. Grapes, cherry tomatoes, and blueberries should be cut lengthways into quarters rather than slices.
When should I introduce a spoon?

You can offer a preloaded spoon from the start of weaning at 6 months. Load the spoon for your baby and let them guide it to their mouth, or let them take the spoon from you. True independent spoon loading, where the baby scoops food themselves, develops gradually from around 12 months and may not be consistent until 18 months or beyond. Neither timeline is a concern; self-loading develops at its own pace.
How should a baby sit for self-feeding?

The high chair position matters for both safety and eating success. Your baby should sit upright, with their back straight and head held steady. Their feet should be supported, either on a footrest or on a surface, not dangling. Dangling feet make it harder to stabilise the trunk, which makes eating harder work. Ensure the tray is close enough that they do not have to lean forward to reach the food.
Is the mess really necessary?

Yes, developmentally speaking. When a baby squeezes, smears, and explores food with their hands, they are building sensory knowledge of that food: its texture, temperature, smell, and weight. This sensory familiarity is part of what leads to eventually eating the food. Research on responsive feeding suggests that allowing messy exploration, rather than restricting or cleaning up mid-meal, is associated with better food acceptance. A splat mat under the high chair saves the floor.
My baby refuses the spoon. What should I do?

Spoon refusal is common, especially in babies who have experienced self-feeding from the start. Try offering a preloaded spoon and letting your baby take it from you, rather than directing the spoon into their mouth. Giving your baby their own spoon to hold while you offer a second preloaded one can work well. Some babies go through a phase of only accepting food from their own hands, and this resolves over time. If your baby is eating adequately via self-feeding, spoon refusal is not a concern.

d.t: Sensory play for babies: what it is, why it matters and how to set it up safely
q: What is sensory play and why is it important for babies?

Sensory play is any activity that engages one or more of a baby's senses: touch, sight, sound, smell, taste, movement, and body awareness. It matters because sensory experiences physically wire the developing brain. Every time a baby touches a new texture, hears a new sound, or moves in a new way, neural connections form and are strengthened. Language, motor skills, emotional regulation, and attention all have roots in early sensory experience.
Is sensory play safe for young babies?

Yes, with appropriate activities and supervision. Newborns and young babies benefit from gentle sensory experiences: skin-to-skin contact, soft fabrics, your face and voice, gentle rocking. The key safety rules that apply to all ages are: never leave a baby alone with sensory materials, ensure nothing is small enough to be a choking hazard, keep water play supervised however shallow, and check for allergies before introducing any food-based play.
What are good sensory play ideas for a four-month-old?

At four months, good sensory activities include offering soft toys of different textures to bat and grasp, holding your baby near crinkling paper or rustling leaves so they can hear and see the movement, placing a small mirror in front of them during tummy time, and taking them outside to experience filtered sunlight, breeze, and the sound of the environment. A few centimetres of warm water in a bowl, with you holding their hands to feel the surface, is a gentle first water experience.
What materials are safe for sensory play with babies?

Safe materials depend on age. For babies under six months: different fabric textures, high-contrast black-and-white visuals, and gentle sounds. For babies from six months: everyday objects in a treasure basket (wooden spoon, silicone cup, cardboard box), small amounts of water in a bowl, and safe musical instruments. Nothing smaller than a toilet roll tube, no latex balloons, no small beads or sensory bin fillers, and no items with sharp edges or strings.
Do I need to buy special sensory toys?

No. The best sensory experiences for babies are almost entirely free: your face, your voice, skin-to-skin contact, bath time, being outside, and a selection of safe household objects. A plastic bowl of warm water with a spoon, a fabric scarf, or a small box of textured fabric scraps offers more genuine sensory variety than most purpose-built sensory kits. Save your money.
How long should sensory play sessions be?

There is no minimum or target duration. Young babies have short attention spans and can become overstimulated quickly. A few minutes of focused sensory engagement, followed by a calm period, is completely appropriate. Watch your baby for cues that they have had enough: looking away, arching their back, fussing, or becoming difficult to soothe are all signals to pause and give them a quiet moment.

d.t: Separate sleep spaces for babies: what the evidence says
q: What does the AAP recommend for newborn sleep?

The AAP recommends that babies sleep on their back, on a firm and flat surface, in their own separate crib or bassinet that meets current safety standards. The sleep space should be free of soft bedding, pillows, bumpers and toys. The AAP advises room-sharing without bed-sharing for at least the first six months and ideally for the first year.
What is the DGKJ's position on infant sleep?

The German Society for Paediatrics and Adolescent Medicine (DGKJ) recommends that babies sleep in their own separate sleep space - a crib or cot placed in the parents' bedroom. The DGKJ advises against bed-sharing and recommends placing babies on their back on a firm, flat mattress without loose bedding for the first year of life.
Is room-sharing without bed-sharing actually safer than a separate room?

Yes. Research cited by the AAP and NHS finds that room-sharing without bed-sharing is associated with a lower risk of SIDS compared with the baby sleeping in a completely separate room. Having the baby close by makes it easier to respond to their needs and to monitor them during the night, while keeping them on a separate safe sleep surface removes the risks associated with bed-sharing.
When can a baby move to their own room?

The AAP recommends room-sharing for at least the first six months and ideally for the first year. After that point, moving a baby to their own room is considered safe if the sleep environment meets safe sleep guidelines - firm, flat surface, no loose bedding, on their back. Both the NHS and the DGKJ follow broadly similar timelines, though guidance varies slightly by country. Always discuss with your health visitor or paediatrician if unsure.

d.t: Separation anxiety in babies: when it starts and what helps
q: At what age does separation anxiety start in babies?
Separation anxiety is common in young children between the ages of 6 months and 3 years. It is a normal part of development and shows that your baby has formed a strong attachment to you.
Is separation anxiety a sign that something is wrong?
No. Separation anxiety is a completely normal stage of development. It shows that your baby recognises and depends on their key caregivers, and understands when those people are not present.
What should I do when my baby gets upset as I leave?

Try to keep goodbyes positive and brief. Smile and wave confidently, as babies can pick up on a parent's own anxiety. Starting with very short separations and gradually increasing the time can also help your baby build confidence.
Can leaving my baby cause lasting harm?
No. Separating from your baby does not cause lasting harm. In fact, managing brief separations helps children develop important independence and coping skills over time.
When should I talk to someone about my baby's separation anxiety?
Speak to your health visitor if your child is very distressed, remains upset for a long time after you leave, or if the behaviour has continued for more than a few weeks without improving.

d.t: Separation anxiety in babies
q: At what age does separation anxiety usually start?

Separation anxiety most often begins between 6 and 8 months, as babies develop a stronger awareness of their primary caregivers. It typically peaks between 10 and 18 months and then gradually eases during the second year.
Is separation anxiety a sign that something is wrong?
No. Separation anxiety is a normal and healthy part of development. It signals that your baby has formed a secure attachment to you, which is exactly what healthy development looks like at this age.
How long do separation anxiety episodes last?

Most babies calm down within a few minutes of a caregiver leaving, especially once they are settled with a familiar person or engaged in play. Brief, consistent goodbyes tend to shorten the distress period.
Can I make separation anxiety worse by comforting my baby?

No. Responding warmly to your baby's distress builds trust and security rather than reinforcing crying. A baby who feels secure with a caregiver is more likely to feel confident exploring independently over time.
When should I talk to a doctor about my baby's separation anxiety?

If anxiety seems extreme, does not ease at all over several months, or if your baby seems distressed even when you are present and not just during separations, it is worth mentioning to your doctor or health visitor. They can rule out other causes and offer reassurance.

d.t: Sex after birth: when it is safe and how to manage common discomfort
q: When is it safe to have sex after giving birth?

There is no single rule, but the general guidance is to wait until lochia (postpartum bleeding) has fully stopped and any stitches or tears have healed, which is usually around 6 weeks. Many couples wait longer, and that is entirely normal.
Why does sex feel different or painful after birth?

Several factors contribute: vaginal dryness caused by lower oestrogen levels (especially during breastfeeding), sensitivity around scar tissue or the perineum, changes to the pelvic floor, and general fatigue. These changes are usually temporary.
What can help with vaginal dryness after birth?

A water-based lubricant is the most straightforward help. If you are breastfeeding, the dryness is linked to low oestrogen and will often improve after weaning. A GP can discuss topical oestrogen options if dryness is significant and persistent.
When should I see a doctor about pain during sex after birth?

If pain during sex persists beyond 3 months postpartum, is getting worse rather than better, or is accompanied by symptoms such as burning, tightness, or muscle spasm (which may indicate vaginismus), it is worth speaking to a GP or women's health physiotherapist.

d.t: Safe sleep: the Red Nose guidelines
q: What does SUDI mean?

SUDI stands for Sudden Unexpected Death in Infancy. It is the term used in Australia to describe any sudden and unexpected death of a baby, including what was previously called SIDS (Sudden Infant Death Syndrome) as well as other causes that are identified after investigation. Red Nose Australia uses SUDI rather than SIDS because it captures a broader category and reflects current medical understanding.
Is it safe for my baby to sleep in my bed in Australia?

Red Nose Australia recommends a separate safe sleep space as the safest option for all babies. Bed-sharing is considered highest risk when a baby is premature or low birth weight, either parent smokes (even outside the home), either parent has consumed alcohol or taken drugs or sedating medication, or the baby is under three months old. Red Nose provides harm-reduction guidance for families who choose to bed-share in other circumstances, but emphasises that no bed-sharing situation is completely without risk.
What cot mattress does Red Nose recommend?

Red Nose Australia recommends a firm, flat, non-tilted mattress that fits the cot snugly with no gaps. The mattress should be covered with a fitted sheet only. Soft, padded, or sagging mattresses are not safe. The cot or bassinet itself should meet Australian Standard AS/NZS 2172 (cots) or AS/NZS 2195 (folding cots and bassinets).
Should my baby wear a hat indoors to sleep?

No. Red Nose Australia advises that babies should not wear hats or hoods indoors during sleep. The head is an important way babies regulate their body temperature and release heat. Covering the head during sleep can cause overheating, which is a known risk factor for SUDI. Hats worn outside for sun protection should be removed before putting your baby down to sleep.
How does Red Nose Australia differ from the UK Lullaby Trust?

Both organisations promote evidence-based safe sleep guidelines and the core recommendations are very similar: back to sleep, clear sleep space, smoke free, room sharing, and breastfeeding if possible. The key differences are in terminology (Red Nose uses SUDI; the Lullaby Trust still uses SIDS more commonly) and bed-sharing guidance. Red Nose Australia takes a more nuanced harm-reduction approach to bed-sharing for lower-risk situations, whereas the UK guidance is more uniformly cautionary about bed-sharing. Australian guidance also places greater emphasis on overheating in warm climates and the use of lower-TOG sleeping bags appropriate for Australian temperatures.

d.t: Signs your baby is hungry or full: feeding cues explained
q: What are the early signs that a baby is hungry?

Early hunger cues include sucking on their fists, licking their lips, and wriggling while opening their mouth as though searching for a breast or bottle. Responding at this stage makes feeding calmer for both of you.
How can I tell when my baby has had enough to eat?

Signs your baby is satisfied include coming off the breast or bottle by themselves, appearing calm and content after the feed, and having cheeks that stay rounded rather than sucking inward during the feed.
How often should I feed my newborn?
In the first few weeks, newborns typically need to feed at least 8 times in 24 hours. Let your baby guide the frequency rather than watching the clock.
What is cluster feeding and is it normal?

Cluster feeding is when your baby wants to feed very frequently, sometimes for long stretches, often in the early months. It is completely normal and commonly linked to growth spurts. Supply adjusts after a few days.
How do I know my baby is getting enough milk?

After the first few days, at least 6 wet nappies a day is a reassuring indicator. From around 5 to 6 days old your baby should also produce at least 2 soft or runny yellow poos a day. Steady weight gain is another positive sign.

d.t: The 6-in-1 vaccine: what it covers and what to expect
q: What diseases does the 6-in-1 vaccine protect against?
The 6-in-1 vaccine protects against diphtheria, hepatitis B, Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b), polio, tetanus, and whooping cough (pertussis).
When does my baby get the 6-in-1 vaccine?
On the NHS schedule, babies receive the 6-in-1 at 8 weeks, 12 weeks, and 16 weeks old. A fourth dose is given at 18 months for babies born on or after 1 July 2024.
What side effects are normal after the 6-in-1 vaccine?
Common reactions include swelling or pain at the injection site, a high temperature, tiredness, loss of appetite, vomiting or diarrhoea, and irritability. These typically settle within a day or two.
When should I seek urgent help after the 6-in-1 vaccine?
Contact your GP or call NHS 111 if your baby is under 3 months old and develops a temperature of 38°C or higher, or if they are aged 3 to 6 months and reach 39°C or higher.
Are there any reasons my baby should not have the 6-in-1 vaccine?

The vaccine should not be given if your baby has had a serious allergic reaction to a previous dose or to specific ingredients including neomycin, polymyxin, formaldehyde, or polysorbate 80. If your baby has a raised temperature on the day, the appointment should be rescheduled. Always tell the nurse or doctor about any existing medical conditions before the jab.

d.t: The six-month sleep regression: causes, signs and how to get through it
q: Is the six-month sleep regression real?

Yes. Around six months many babies experience a period of disrupted sleep that had previously been improving. The disruption is driven by real developmental changes: a burst in brain development, increased awareness of the world, the start of nap consolidation from three naps to two, and often the beginnings of teething. It is a recognised pattern, not a random bad patch.
How is the six-month regression different from the four-month regression?

The four-month regression involves a permanent change in sleep architecture: your baby's sleep cycles mature and they start cycling between light and deep sleep in a more adult-like pattern, which they cannot unlearn. The six-month regression, by contrast, is a temporary disruption. Your baby's sleep architecture does not change; the disruption is caused by developmental activity and nap transition, not a structural shift. This means the six-month regression tends to pass more quickly and more completely once the underlying cause settles.
How long does the six-month sleep regression last?

For most babies, two to four weeks. Some babies sail through in less than two weeks with only mild disruption. For others, particularly if nap consolidation is happening at the same time, it can feel like it stretches to a month. If sleep is still significantly disrupted after four to six weeks, it is worth thinking about whether something else is at play, or whether a habit that formed during the regression is now the main driver.
Should I drop to two naps during the six-month regression?

Many babies do naturally transition from three naps to two naps around this age, and the regression and nap transition often happen together. If your baby is consistently refusing the third nap, or the third nap is interfering with bedtime, it may be time to make the move to two naps. If all three naps are still happening reasonably well, it is fine to keep them for now and wait for the clearer nap-drop signals to arrive.
What makes the six-month regression worse?

Overtiredness is the main thing that prolongs and deepens the disruption. If naps are falling apart and your baby is accumulating sleep debt, nights get harder. Keeping wake windows age-appropriate (roughly 2 to 2.5 hours at this age), protecting at least one quality nap in the cot, and adjusting bedtime earlier temporarily can all help prevent overtiredness from compounding the regression.
Does teething cause the six-month regression?

Teething can contribute to sleep disruption around this age, but it is rarely the sole cause. The first teeth typically appear between four and eight months, so some six-month-olds are beginning to feel early teething discomfort. If your baby is drooling heavily, chewing on everything and irritable, teething may be adding to the picture. The regression itself, however, is primarily driven by developmental and nap-transition factors rather than teething alone.

d.t: Your postnatal six-week check: what happens and what to raise
q: What happens at the six-week postnatal check for the mother?

The GP checks your physical recovery including wound healing, asks about your mental health using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, discusses contraception, and reviews how feeding is going. It is also a chance to raise any concerns you have not yet mentioned.
What is checked at the baby's six-week check?

The doctor checks the baby's weight and growth, heart sounds, hip stability (to screen for developmental dysplasia), eyes, reflexes, and genitals. They will also ask about feeding, sleeping, and how the baby is developing overall.
What should I raise at my six-week check if the doctor doesn't ask?

Bring up any pelvic floor symptoms such as leaking or urgency, any pain during sex, low mood or anxiety that has persisted beyond the first two weeks, feeding difficulties, and concerns about your scar if you had stitches or a caesarean.
What if I cannot get a six-week check appointment?

Contact your GP surgery to request the appointment as a clinical need, not a routine review. If there are significant delays, speak to your midwife or health visitor, who can flag the need. You should not have to wait more than 8 weeks.

d.t: Sleep associations and props: what they are and whether you need to change them
q: What is a sleep association?

A sleep association is any condition that is reliably present when a baby or child falls asleep. It might be feeding, rocking, a dummy, music, your physical presence, a white noise machine, or a particular toy. Humans of all ages associate certain conditions with sleep, and for babies these associations form quickly and become strong. They are not problems in themselves; they only become worth addressing if you find them unsustainable to continue.
Is feeding to sleep a bad habit?

No. Feeding to sleep is biologically normal and highly effective. Many parents feed to sleep for months or years without any difficulty. The one practical consequence is that if a baby wakes at night in a light sleep phase and feeding is what they associate with falling asleep, they will want to feed to get back to sleep. This is only a problem if it is happening more frequently than you can sustain, or if supply is dropping and the feed no longer settles them. If it works for your family, it is a valid and nurturing approach.
What is the difference between a sleep association and a sleep prop?

The terms are often used interchangeably. A sleep prop typically implies something external that is required to initiate sleep, while a sleep association is the broader category of anything the brain links with falling asleep. All sleep props are sleep associations, but some sleep associations involve the parent's presence or actions rather than an object. Neither term implies the association needs to be removed; both just describe what is happening.
Which sleep associations have safety concerns?

Loose soft toys, blankets, pillows, and bumper pads in the cot are safety concerns for babies under 12 months. A dummy used during sleep is associated with a reduced SIDS risk, not a higher one, and is considered safe. The parent's physical presence is safe in the sense that it does not pose a hazard, though bed-sharing on a soft mattress or with a tired adult carries its own risks. White noise used at appropriate volume and distance is safe.
How do I change a sleep association I no longer want to continue?

Gradual change tends to be gentler than abrupt removal. For feeding to sleep, you might feed until drowsy then unlatch just before the baby is fully asleep, extending this gap a little further over several nights. For rocking, you might slow the rocking gradually and eventually move to swaying, then stillness. For parental presence, fading involves staying close but becoming less involved over several nights. The key is small steps with enough time between them for the baby to adjust.
At what age do babies become capable of falling asleep without help?

There is no universal age. Some babies naturally begin falling asleep with less help from around 3 to 4 months as their sleep architecture matures; others rely on assistance for much longer and this is completely normal. Developmental readiness varies widely. Many parents find the six to eight month range is when their baby first shows signs of being able to fall asleep independently if given the opportunity, but this is not a rule.

d.t: Sleep deprivation as a new parent: effects and how to cope
q: How long does the exhausting phase of newborn night waking last?

There is no fixed timeline, but the NHS notes that the phase when your baby wakes several times a night will not last forever. As babies get older, they sleep for longer periods, and most parents notice a gradual improvement across the first months.
Is it safe to sleep when the baby sleeps?

Yes. The NHS recommends resting during your baby's sleep rather than using that time for housework. If you are worried about oversleeping, set an alarm before you lie down so you can close your eyes without that concern.
Can my partner help with night feeds if I am breastfeeding?

Once you have a good breastfeeding routine established, your partner can occasionally give a bottle of expressed breast milk during the night. Partners can also take on nappy changes and resettling so the breastfeeding parent gets back to sleep more quickly.
When should I be concerned that tiredness is something more serious?

If you cannot sleep at night even when your baby is asleep, feel tired all the time, feel persistently low or hopeless, or have lost interest in things you normally enjoy, these can be signs of postnatal depression. Speak to your GP or midwife as soon as possible.
What quick relaxation can help when I cannot get a full sleep?

The NHS suggests that as little as 5 to 10 minutes of deep relaxation can help refresh you. Spending around 30 minutes on a calming activity before you try to sleep, such as slow breathing or gentle stretching, can also make it easier to fall asleep when you do get the chance.

d.t: Baby and toddler sleep environment: temperature, darkness and white noise
q: What temperature should a baby's room be for sleep?

NHS guidance recommends keeping the room your baby sleeps in between 16 and 20 degrees Celsius. This range reduces the risk of overheating, which is an independent risk factor for SIDS. The easiest way to monitor this is with a simple room thermometer placed near the cot, away from direct sunlight or heat sources.
Do I need a completely dark room for my baby to sleep?

Near-total darkness is genuinely helpful for sleep. The absence of light triggers the release of melatonin, the hormone that cues the body to sleep. Blackout blinds or blackout liners make a particularly big difference in summer when evenings stay light, and for early morning wake-ups caused by dawn light. That said, a very faint nightlight for your own navigation is fine and will not disrupt sleep in most babies.
Is white noise safe for babies?

White noise can help some babies settle and stay asleep, but volume matters. Research has shown that some commercially available white noise machines can exceed 85 decibels at close range, which is above safe limits for infants. Keep any white noise source at least 2 metres from the cot and cap the volume at around 50 decibels (roughly the level of a quiet shower). It is a useful tool for some families but not essential for all.
What TOG rating does my baby need?

TOG rating measures warmth. In a room at 16 to 20 degrees Celsius, a 2.5 TOG sleeping bag is suitable for most of the year. At 20 to 24 degrees, a 1 TOG bag is more appropriate. Above 24 degrees, a 0.5 TOG or a lightweight swaddle is usually enough. Always combine the TOG of the sleeping bag with the vest or sleepsuit underneath when assessing whether your baby will be comfortable.
Does white noise need to stay on all night?

It does not have to. Some parents use white noise only during the settling period and let it switch off once the baby is asleep. Others run it all night as a way of masking household sounds that might cause waking. Both approaches work. If you run it all night, the 50 decibel volume limit and 2-metre distance from the cot still apply.
Can I use essential oils or air fresheners in my baby's room?

It is best to avoid fragrance in the sleep environment altogether. Strong scents can irritate a baby's sensitive airways and may trigger sneezing or congestion that disrupts sleep. Plug-in air fresheners, scented candles, essential oil diffusers, and heavily fragranced fabric softeners are all worth avoiding in the room where your baby sleeps.

d.t: Sleep training: what different approaches involve and what the evidence says
q: Is sleep training safe for babies?

The current body of evidence, including studies published in Pediatrics and reviews by the American Academy of Pediatrics, has found no evidence that behavioural sleep training methods cause lasting psychological harm, increase infant stress hormones over time, or damage the parent-child attachment relationship. A 2016 randomised controlled trial by Price and colleagues found no differences in emotional or behavioural outcomes, stress hormones, or attachment between sleep-trained and non-sleep-trained children at age five. That said, individual families differ, and what feels right for one family may not suit another. If you have concerns, speaking with your paediatrician or health visitor is the best next step.
What age can I start sleep training?

Most sleep specialists and paediatric bodies suggest waiting until at least four to six months before attempting any form of sleep training. Before this age, babies have limited capacity for self-regulation and most still genuinely need night feeds. The American Academy of Pediatrics and NHS guidance both emphasise that frequent night waking in the early months is normal and expected. Once a baby has reached a consistent developmental readiness, which is often around four to six months but varies between individuals, sleep training approaches are more likely to be effective and appropriate.
Will sleep training cause my baby lasting stress or harm their attachment to me?

Research to date has not found evidence that sleep training causes lasting stress or damages the attachment relationship between parent and child. The largest randomised controlled trial on this question, published in 2016, followed children to age five and found no significant differences in cortisol levels, attachment security, emotional regulation, or behaviour between sleep-trained and control groups. Attachment is built through thousands of everyday moments of warmth, responsiveness and connection, not by a single sleep training period. If you find any method too distressing for you or your baby, stopping and trying a gentler approach is always a valid choice.
What if none of the sleep training methods work for my family?

It is entirely normal for some families to try a method and find it does not suit their baby's temperament or their own values and wellbeing. Babies differ widely in their sleep patterns, and some children naturally take longer to consolidate overnight sleep regardless of the approach used. If you have tried several methods without success, or if sleep deprivation is significantly affecting your or your baby's health, it is worth speaking to your GP, paediatrician, or a certified paediatric sleep consultant. Some families also find that a combination of approaches, or simply continuing to respond to their baby's needs while waiting for developmental maturity, is the right path for them.

d.t: Sleep training methods: a calm comparison of the main approaches
q: Is sleep training safe?

Yes, when done at an age-appropriate stage, sleep training is considered safe by the American Academy of Pediatrics. All methods assume a safe sleep environment: a firm, flat surface, back-sleeping, and nothing loose in the crib. Long-term studies, including Price et al. (Pediatrics, 2012), found no evidence of lasting harm to children's emotional wellbeing, stress levels, or the parent-child relationship.
What age should you start sleep training?

Most experts recommend waiting until at least 4 to 6 months, because before that age a baby's sleep architecture is not yet mature enough to support independent settling. The most common starting point is 5 to 8 months. Premature babies should be assessed by corrected age rather than birth age.
Does cry it out cause lasting harm?

Multiple high-quality studies, including Price et al. (Pediatrics, 2012) with a five-year follow-up, found no evidence of lasting emotional harm, increased stress levels, or damage to the parent-child attachment when extinction-based methods are used at the appropriate developmental stage. The Middlemiss et al. (Early Human Development, 2012) study showed that cortisol responses can become asynchronous during training, which is why researchers recommend ensuring the approach is developmentally appropriate and used within a loving, responsive relationship overall.
Which sleep training method is fastest?

Full extinction (cry it out) tends to produce the fastest results, often within 3 to 5 nights, because there is no variability in the response for the baby to learn from. The Ferber method is close behind and is the most studied. Gentler methods like fading and the chair method are slower, typically taking one to three weeks. Speed is one factor, but so is what you and your baby can sustain.
What if my baby vomits during sleep training?

Vomiting during prolonged crying can happen. If it does, go in calmly, clean up as matter-of-factly as you can with minimal interaction, settle your baby, and leave again. Try not to treat vomiting as a signal to abandon the process unless your baby seems unwell, as doing so can teach the baby that vomiting ends the training. If vomiting is frequent or your baby seems distressed beyond normal settling, pause and speak to your health visitor or doctor.
Is it okay not to sleep train?

Absolutely. Sleep training is a choice, not a requirement. Many families use responsive settling approaches throughout infancy and find that sleep naturally consolidates as the baby develops. What matters most is that everyone in your household is getting enough rest to function and that your approach feels right for your family. There is no single correct way to help a baby sleep.

d.t: Soothing a crying baby and coping with colic
q: How do I know if my baby has colic?

Colic is typically defined as crying for more than 3 hours a day, more than 3 days a week, for more than 3 weeks, in a baby who is otherwise healthy and gaining weight. If you are unsure, speak to your GP or health visitor to rule out other causes.
When does colic peak and when does it stop?
Colic typically peaks around 6-8 weeks of age and usually resolves by 3-4 months. It can feel relentless in the moment, but the vast majority of cases clear up as the digestive system matures.
Is it safe to put my baby down and take a short break?

Yes. If you feel overwhelmed, it is safe to place your baby in their cot on their back and leave the room for a few minutes. Making sure you are calm before returning is better for both of you. Never shake a baby.
When should I call the doctor about crying?

Contact your GP or NHS 111 if your baby has a high-pitched or unusual cry that sounds different from normal, if crying comes with fever, if your baby is not feeding, appears pale or limp, or if you are worried for any reason. Trust your instincts.

d.t: When to start solids: weaning around 6 months
q: What are the three signs my baby is ready for solids?

All three must be present: sitting with support and holding their head steady; coordinating eyes, hands, and mouth to reach for and put food in their mouth; and swallowing food rather than pushing it back out with their tongue. If only one or two signs are there, wait a little longer and check again.
Should I do baby-led weaning or spoon-feeding?

Either approach works, and many families use both. NHS does not recommend one over the other. Whichever you choose, the key is to progress toward lumpier textures and soft finger foods by around 9 months.
How much food should a 6-month-old eat at first?

Very small amounts, often just a few teaspoons at one meal per day. Some days a baby may eat very little or refuse entirely, and that is normal. Appetite for solid food builds gradually over several weeks. Milk remains the main source of nutrition.
What should I offer at the very first meal?

A small amount of a single soft food: a teaspoon of smooth sweet potato puree, mashed ripe banana, or soft cooked carrot, for example. Offering one food at a time at first makes it easier to spot any reaction before moving on to more variety.

d.t: Starting solids: NHMRC guidance
q: When should Australian babies start solid foods?

The NHMRC recommends introducing solid foods at around 6 months of age, alongside breast milk or infant formula. Solids should not be introduced before 4 months. There is no need to rush: starting at around 6 months is the evidence-based recommendation for most babies. If your baby was born prematurely, speak with your Maternal and Child Health nurse or GP before introducing solids.
What are the best first foods for Australian babies?

The NHMRC and Healthdirect Australia recommend starting with iron-rich foods: pureed or mashed meat (such as chicken, beef, or lamb), cooked and pureed legumes (such as lentils and chickpeas), and iron-fortified infant cereals. You can then broaden out to pureed or mashed vegetables and fruit. Avocado is a nutritious and easy first food popular with Australian families.
Do I need to avoid allergens when starting solids?

No. The ASCIA (Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy) guidelines recommend introducing common allergenic foods early, around 6 months, and continuing to offer them regularly. Avoiding allergenic foods does not reduce allergy risk and may actually increase it. If your baby already has severe eczema or a known food allergy, speak with your GP or allergy specialist before introducing allergenic foods.
Can I give my baby Vegemite?

Vegemite is very high in salt and is not suitable for babies under 12 months. The NHMRC recommends no added salt in food for babies in the first year of life. Once your baby turns 12 months, a very thin scraping may be offered occasionally, but it should not be a regular part of their diet.
Where can I get help with starting solids in Australia?

Contact Healthdirect Australia on 1800 022 222 (24 hours, 7 days) for free health advice from a registered nurse. Your Maternal and Child Health (MCH) nurse is another excellent first point of contact. State health departments including NSW Health, VIC Health, and Queensland Health all publish free resources aligned with NHMRC guidance. Your GP can provide a referral to a paediatric dietitian if your baby has complex feeding needs.

d.t: Starting solids at 6 months: a step-by-step guide for the first weeks
q: How do I know my baby is ready for solids?

There are three physical signs to look for: your baby can sit upright and hold their head steady without much support; they have good control of their head and neck; and they have lost the tongue-thrust reflex that pushes food out of the mouth. All three should be present. Watching food or putting things in their mouth is normal baby behaviour at any age and is not a readiness sign on its own.
Is 6 months too late to start solids?

No. The NHS and WHO recommend introducing solids at around 6 months. Starting before 4 months is not recommended as the gut is not ready. Anywhere in the 6-month window is appropriate once the three readiness signs are present. If you have concerns about timing, speak to your health visitor.
How much should a baby eat in the first weeks of weaning?

Very little, and that is completely expected. The goal in the first two to four weeks is for your baby to experience new tastes and textures, not to eat a set amount. Milk remains the main source of nutrition throughout the first year. Start with one small meal a day, and let your baby guide how much they take.
What should I offer as a first food?

Iron-rich foods should feature from day one, because a baby's iron stores from birth begin to run low at around 6 months and milk alone cannot replenish them. Good choices include well-cooked, pureed or mashed meat, mashed cooked lentils, mashed egg yolk, or iron-fortified baby cereal. Pair these alongside soft vegetables and fruit.
My baby keeps gagging. Should I stop?

Gagging is a normal protective reflex, not choking. It looks alarming but it is the baby's airway protecting itself by pushing food forward. Most babies gag frequently in the early weeks of weaning. Stay calm, let them work through it, and do not rush in to remove food. Choking, by contrast, is silent and requires immediate action. Learning the difference, and basic infant first aid, is worthwhile before you begin.
Should I give my baby water when I start solids?

Yes. Small sips of cooled boiled water from an open cup or a free-flow beaker can be offered with meals from 6 months. This helps the baby get used to drinking from a cup and supports good oral hygiene habits. Do not use a bottle for water, as it can become a comfort habit. Keep amounts small, as milk is still the main fluid source.
What if my baby refuses everything I offer?

Refusal is very common at the start. Babies may need to see and smell a new food many times before accepting it. Keep offering calmly, without pressure or coaxing. Try different times of day, when your baby is alert but not overtired or ravenous. It can take ten or more exposures before a baby accepts a new food. If refusal continues across many weeks or you have concerns about growth, speak to your health visitor.

d.t: Vaccine schedule from birth to 14 months: what to expect
q: How many vaccines does my baby need in the first year?

The STIKO schedule calls for multiple vaccine appointments in the first 14 months. In Germany, babies typically receive vaccines at 6 weeks (rotavirus oral drops), then at 2 months, 4 months, and 11 months (hexavalent and pneumococcal), with meningococcal B doses at 3, 4, and 12 months, meningococcal C at 12 months, and MMR with varicella at 11 months. In total this covers ten disease groups across roughly seven to eight clinic visits, many of which involve combination vaccines so the number of injections at any one visit is kept as low as possible.
Can I split vaccines to reduce stress on my baby?

Splitting combination vaccines is not recommended by STIKO. Combination products such as the hexavalent vaccine are designed to deliver strong, coordinated immunity and have an excellent safety record. Splitting doses means more appointments, more individual injections overall, and leaves gaps in protection during the intervals between split doses. If you are worried about your baby's comfort, discuss pain management strategies with your paediatrician, such as breastfeeding during the injection, skin-to-skin contact, or distraction techniques.
What should I do if my baby has a fever after vaccination?

A mild fever of up to 38.5 degrees Celsius in the 24 to 48 hours after vaccination is a normal immune response. Keep your baby comfortable, offer extra feeds, and use age-appropriate paracetamol or ibuprofen if recommended by your paediatrician. Contact your doctor promptly if the fever exceeds 39 degrees Celsius, lasts more than 48 hours, your baby is inconsolably crying for more than three hours, or you notice a spreading rash, difficulty breathing, or any sign of serious illness.
Does Cubby track the vaccination schedule?

Yes. Cubby includes a built-in vaccine tracker that follows the STIKO recommended schedule. You can log each dose as it is given, receive reminders before upcoming appointments, and view your baby's full vaccination history at any time. Open the app and go to the Health section to get started.

d.t: Sun protection for babies under 12 months
q: Can I put sunscreen on a baby under 6 months?

The NHS advises keeping babies under 6 months out of direct strong sunlight entirely. Shade and protective clothing are the primary defences at this age. Where any skin is unavoidably exposed, consult your health visitor about whether sunscreen is appropriate.
What SPF sunscreen should I use for my baby?
The NHS recommends at least SPF 30 for children, along with a 4-star UVA rating (or the UVA circle logo). Sunscreen is not a substitute for shade and clothing; it should be used alongside them.
When is the sun strongest and most risky for babies?
In the UK, UV levels are highest between 11am and 3pm from March to October, and when the UV index reaches 3 or above. This is the window when shade matters most for young babies.
How often should I reapply sunscreen on my baby?

The NHS recommends reapplying sunscreen every 2 hours, and again immediately after the baby has been near water, is sweating, or has been dried with a towel. Even water-resistant formulas need reapplying after water contact.
Does cloud cover mean my baby is safe from the sun?
Not necessarily. UV rays can still reach the ground on overcast days. If the UV index is 3 or above, the same shade, clothing and sunscreen precautions apply even when skies look cloudy.

d.t: Sun safety for babies: UV, shade and clothing
q: Can I put sunscreen on my baby in Australia?

It depends on your baby's age. Cancer Council Australia advises keeping babies under 6 months out of direct sun altogether and not applying sunscreen to them: their skin is too sensitive, and shade plus protective clothing should be used instead. From 6 months of age, sunscreen is appropriate and recommended as part of a broader sun protection routine alongside clothing, shade, and a wide-brimmed hat.
What SPF sunscreen should I use for my baby in Australia?

Cancer Council Australia recommends SPF 50+ broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen for babies from 6 months of age. SPF 50+ gives the highest level of UVB protection available, and broad spectrum means it also protects against UVA rays. Apply 20 minutes before going outside and reapply at least every 2 hours, and immediately after swimming or towel drying.
What UV Index requires sun protection in Australia?

SunSmart and Cancer Council Australia recommend sun protection whenever the UV Index reaches 3 or above. This is classed as Moderate on the scale. In most parts of Australia, the UV Index exceeds 3 for most of the year, including in winter and on cloudy days. The SunSmart Global UV app gives you a free daily forecast for your exact location so you always know when protection is needed.
How do I protect my newborn from the Australian sun?

For newborns and babies under 6 months, Cancer Council Australia recommends avoiding direct sun exposure as much as possible. Keep your baby in the shade at all times outdoors: use a pram hood or shade cloth, position under trees or buildings, and avoid outdoor time during the peak UV hours of 10am to 2pm (11am to 3pm during daylight saving). Dress your baby in lightweight sun-protective clothing (UPF 50+) covering as much skin as possible, and use a wide-brimmed hat. Do not apply sunscreen to babies under 6 months.
Do Australian babies still need vitamin D supplements?

Yes, many Australian babies do still need vitamin D supplements, particularly if they are exclusively breastfed. Breast milk contains very little vitamin D, and correct sun protection practices for babies mean they are not producing much through the skin either. Australian and international guidelines recommend 400 IU of vitamin D per day for breastfed babies. Speak with your GP or Child and Family Health Nurse about whether supplementation is right for your baby.

d.t: Sun safety for babies: protecting delicate skin in warm climates
q: Can I put sunscreen on a baby under 6 months?

The AAP recommends keeping babies under 6 months out of direct sunlight and using shade, hats, and lightweight clothing as the primary protection. Sunscreen should be avoided on newborns and very young babies because their skin absorbs chemicals more readily and is more sensitive to reactions. In small amounts on exposed areas that cannot be covered, such as the face and backs of hands, a mineral sunscreen with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide may be used if sun avoidance is not possible, but this should only be done as a last resort and after discussing with your paediatrician.
What SPF sunscreen is recommended for babies from 6 months?

The AAP recommends a broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher for babies from 6 months, and many paediatric dermatologists suggest SPF 50 or higher in very sunny conditions. Choose a mineral sunscreen containing zinc oxide or titanium dioxide rather than a chemical sunscreen, as mineral formulas sit on top of the skin rather than being absorbed and are less likely to irritate sensitive infant skin. Apply generously to all exposed areas at least 15 minutes before going outside and reapply every 2 hours, or immediately after swimming or towel drying.
What are the peak UV hours and how should I plan outings?

UV radiation is strongest between 10 am and 4 pm, regardless of temperature or cloud cover. In warm, sunny climates the UV index regularly reaches 8 or above during these hours, which is classified as Very High to Extreme by the World Health Organization. Planning outings in the early morning (before 10 am) or late afternoon (after 4 pm) significantly reduces your baby's UV exposure. On days when the UV index is 6 or higher, the WHO recommends full sun protection for everyone, and for babies this means shade, hat, UPF clothing, and sunscreen from 6 months combined.
Does a cloudy day mean my baby is safe from UV rays?

No. Clouds block visible light but do not block UV radiation effectively. Up to 80 percent of UV rays pass through light cloud cover. UV also reflects off sand, water, and light-coloured surfaces such as white walls and pavements, increasing total exposure even in shade near these surfaces. Always apply sun protection measures based on the UV index forecast, not on how bright or warm the day feels. Many weather apps and national meteorology services publish daily UV index forecasts that make it easy to check before heading out.

d.t: Sure Start Maternity Grant: who can claim and how to apply
q: Who qualifies for the Sure Start Maternity Grant?

You or your partner must be receiving a qualifying benefit to be eligible. Qualifying benefits include Universal Credit, Income Support, income-based Jobseeker's Allowance, income-related Employment and Support Allowance, Child Tax Credit (at a rate higher than the family element), Working Tax Credit that includes a disability or severe disability element, or Pension Credit. You must also usually be expecting your first child, or be expecting a multiple birth (twins or more) even if you already have children.
How do I claim the Sure Start Maternity Grant?

You need to complete form SF100, which is available to download from GOV.UK or to pick up from your nearest Jobcentre Plus. The form needs to be signed by a healthcare professional (your GP, midwife, or health visitor) to confirm your pregnancy or the birth. Once completed, you can return it by post or in person to your Jobcentre Plus. You cannot claim online at present.
When should I claim the Sure Start Maternity Grant?

You can claim from 11 weeks before your due date up to 3 months after your baby is born. Waiting until after the birth is a common mistake: you are entitled to claim before your baby arrives, and claiming early means you receive the payment sooner. For adoptions, you can claim from the date of the adoption order up to 3 months after that date.
Can I claim if this is not my first baby?

Usually no. The Sure Start Maternity Grant is only available for your first child. However, if you are expecting a multiple birth (twins, triplets, or more) and you already have children, you can still claim because the grant is available for multiple births regardless of existing children. If you are not sure whether you qualify, contact your Jobcentre Plus or the Universal Credit helpline.
What is the Best Start Grant in Scotland?

If you live in Scotland, the Sure Start Maternity Grant does not apply to you. Instead, Scotland has the Best Start Grant, which is administered by Social Security Scotland. The Best Start Grant has three payments: a Pregnancy and Baby Payment, a First Birthday Payment, and a Early Learning Payment. The eligibility rules are similar to the SSMG but the payments are higher and the qualifying benefits list is wider. Apply at mygov.scot or by calling Social Security Scotland.

d.t: Swaddling a baby: technique, benefits and when to stop
q: What fabric should I use to swaddle my baby?
Lightweight materials such as thin muslin are recommended. Heavier fabrics can cause overheating, which is a SIDS risk factor. Keep layers under the swaddle to a minimum as well.
Can swaddling cause hip problems?

Wrapping too tightly around the hips can increase the risk of developmental dysplasia of the hip. The wrap should always leave room for the hips to move freely and naturally, while keeping the torso snug.
When should I stop swaddling my baby?

You should stop wrapping your baby's arms inside a swaddle as soon as you notice any signs that they can roll over. A baby who rolls face-down while swaddled cannot push themselves back and may be at risk of suffocation.
Is it safe to swaddle during bed-sharing?
No. Swaddling is not recommended during bed-sharing or co-sleeping. If you are sharing a sleep surface with your baby, use a baby sleeping bag instead.
Should my baby's head be covered when swaddled?
No. The head should always remain uncovered when your baby is swaddled. Covering the head can cause overheating and increase the risk of SIDS.

d.t: Swaddling your baby: how to do it safely
q: Does swaddling cause hip dysplasia?

Tight swaddling with legs held straight and together can restrict normal hip development and raise the risk of hip dysplasia. Hip-healthy swaddling keeps the legs free to bend up and out at the hips. The International Hip Dysplasia Institute recommends always using a technique that allows natural leg movement.
When should I stop swaddling my baby?

Stop swaddling as soon as your baby shows any sign of rolling, which can happen from around 8 weeks but sometimes earlier. A swaddled baby who rolls onto their stomach cannot push themselves back and faces a serious suffocation risk. Most babies are ready to transition out of a swaddle by 2 to 3 months.
Can I swaddle my baby for sleep?

Yes, swaddling can help newborns settle to sleep by reducing the startle reflex. Always place a swaddled baby on their back on a firm flat surface, never on their side or stomach. Ensure the swaddle is not so tight that the chest cannot expand freely, and check that the baby is not overheating.
What is the best fabric for a swaddle?

A lightweight, breathable fabric such as muslin cotton is ideal. It allows air to circulate and reduces the risk of overheating, which is a key safe-sleep concern. Avoid thick fleece or multiple layers. A single muslin square that is about 120 cm by 120 cm gives you enough fabric to wrap comfortably without excess bulk.

d.t: Swaddling your baby: how to do it safely and when to stop
q: When should I stop swaddling my baby?

You should stop swaddling as soon as your baby shows any signs of rolling, which typically happens between two and four months of age. If a swaddled baby rolls onto their front and cannot roll back, they may be unable to lift their head and could suffocate. Continuing to swaddle after rolling begins significantly increases this risk.
How do I know if my swaddle is too tight?

A correctly wrapped swaddle should feel snug around the arms and torso but never restrict breathing or chest movement. You should be able to slide two fingers between the swaddle and your baby's chest. The hips must always have room to move freely, bending up and out. A swaddle that holds the legs straight or pressed together is too tight around the hips and can contribute to hip dysplasia.
Can swaddling cause overheating?

Yes, overheating is a real risk with swaddling. Use only lightweight, breathable fabric such as muslin or thin cotton. Keep the room temperature between 16 and 20 degrees Celsius (61 to 68 Fahrenheit). A swaddled baby should wear just a nappy or a single light layer underneath. Check your baby's temperature at the back of the neck or tummy: warm and dry is right; hot, sweaty, or flushed means they need less.
What is the safest way to transition out of the swaddle?

The gentlest transition is to leave one arm free while keeping the other swaddled for a few nights, then move to both arms free. Some families use a transitional sleep sack with a firm but flexible body section that gives a similar contained feeling without restricting arm movement. Consistency and patience help: most babies adjust within one to two weeks.

d.t: Swimming lessons for babies: when to start and what to look for
q: What age can babies start swimming lessons?

Many programs in Australia accept babies from around 3 to 4 months, once they have reasonable head control. The AAP notes that formal swimming programs can reduce drowning risk in children from age 1 onward, but younger babies can still benefit from water familiarisation classes with a parent present.
Can babies drown silently? Is pool time ever safe?

Drowning is fast, silent, and can occur in very shallow water. A baby should never be left unsupervised near any water, including baths. In a class setting, a parent or carer should be in the water with the baby at all times. Touch supervision means being within arm's reach.
What should I look for in a baby swimming instructor?

In Australia, look for instructors holding an AUSTSWIM Teacher of Swimming and Water Safety qualification or an equivalent Swimming Australia accreditation. Classes should be small, warm (at least 30 to 32 degrees Celsius for babies), and focused on water familiarisation and parent-child bonding rather than forced submersion.
Should a baby be dunked underwater?

Involuntary or forced submersion is not recommended. Reputable programs focus on gradual water familiarisation. Submersions in quality classes are very brief, always cued, and never forced. The Royal Life Saving Society Australia advises choosing programs that do not use forced submersion techniques.

d.t: Swimming and water safety for babies: when to start and how to stay safe
q: When can I take my baby swimming for the first time?

Most guidelines suggest babies can start swimming from around 6 weeks of age, provided your doctor or midwife has given the all-clear after the postnatal check. Some health authorities recommend waiting until the primary vaccination schedule is more complete (around 2 months) to reduce infection risk in public pools. Always get individual guidance from your health professional before your first pool visit.
What water temperature is safe for babies in a pool?

Babies lose body heat quickly, so pool water should be warm enough to prevent chilling. A temperature of 32 to 35 degrees Celsius is generally recommended for infant swimming programs. Most dedicated parent-and-baby classes use heated pools in this range. If your baby starts shivering, has pale or mottled skin, or becomes very quiet, take them out immediately and warm them gently with a towel.
Do infant swimming classes prevent drowning?

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) notes that formal swimming instruction does not drown-proof any child, including babies. However, evidence suggests that participation in formal swimming lessons may reduce the risk of drowning in children aged 1 to 4 years. Regardless of swimming ability or lessons, constant arm's-reach supervision near any water remains the most critical safety measure at all ages.
Should I let my baby go underwater during a swimming class?

Voluntary submersion during parent-and-baby classes is common in many programs and can be done safely by trained instructors. Babies have a natural breath-holding reflex (the diving reflex) that is strongest in the first months of life. However, involuntary or forced submersion carries risks. Discuss the specific approach with the instructor before the session and ensure the class follows nationally recognised guidelines from bodies such as the Royal Life Saving Society Australia or the Japanese Swimming Federation.

d.t: Tagesmutter or Krippe: choosing childcare for your baby
q: From what age does my child have a legal right to a childcare place?

Children in Germany have a legal entitlement (Rechtsanspruch) to a childcare place from the age of one. Before that, parents can still apply, but the entitlement only kicks in at 12 months. In practice, many families start the search during pregnancy because waiting lists can be long.
How much does a Krippe or Tagesmutter place cost?

Costs vary by federal state and municipality. Most families pay an income-related parental contribution (Elternbeitrag) that is calculated by the local Jugendamt. In some cities, such as Berlin, childcare is fully subsidised for families using the Kita-Gutschein voucher system. Always ask your local Jugendamt for the current fee schedule that applies to your household income.
What is a Kita-Gutschein and how do I get one?

A Kita-Gutschein (childcare voucher) is issued by the Jugendamt in certain cities -- including Berlin and Hamburg -- and confirms your entitlement to a subsidised childcare place. You apply through your local Jugendamt, usually once your child turns one or slightly before. The voucher specifies the number of hours funded per day and can be used at an approved Krippe or with an approved Tagesmutter.
Who approves and oversees a Tagesmutter?

The Jugendamt (youth welfare office) in each district is responsible for issuing licences to childminders and monitoring their practice. A licensed Tagesmutter must complete a recognised training course, pass a suitability assessment, and have their home inspected. They are allowed to care for up to five children at a time from different families.

d.t: TCM approaches to colic in babies: what the evidence says
q: Does tui na massage help with colic?

Some small clinical studies have found that infant massage, including tui na-style abdominal massage, can reduce crying duration compared with no intervention. However, the evidence base is limited: most studies are small, of short duration, and not always well-blinded. Tui na massage is very low risk when performed gently, so many families try it as a complementary measure alongside the approaches recommended by their GP or health visitor.
Are herbal remedies safe for colic in young babies?

Many herbal preparations traditionally used for infant colic have not been studied adequately for safety or efficacy in babies under three months. Some carry real risks, including contamination, sedation, or allergic reactions. The NHS advises against giving herbal remedies to young babies without medical guidance. Always tell your doctor about any herbal preparation you are considering.
Is acupuncture safe for newborns?

A small number of randomised trials have examined acupuncture or laser acupuncture for infant colic with mixed results. The evidence is not strong enough to draw firm conclusions. Adverse events in the published literature are rare but include minor local reactions. If you are considering acupuncture for a young baby, seek a practitioner with specific paediatric training and inform your health visitor or GP.
When should I see a doctor about colic?

If your baby cries for more than three hours a day, more than three days a week, for more than three weeks, discuss this with your GP or health visitor. They can rule out causes such as reflux, cow's milk protein allergy, or other conditions before you explore any complementary approaches. Colic that comes with a fever, vomiting, blood in stools, or a baby who is not gaining weight needs urgent medical assessment.

d.t: The witching hour in babies: what it is and how to cope
q: What is the witching hour in babies?

The witching hour refers to a stretch of time, often in the late afternoon or evening, when a baby cries much more than usual without an obvious reason. It is closely linked to colic, which the NHS describes as a baby crying a lot with no clear cause.
When does the witching hour start and end?
Crying episodes tend to be most intense in the afternoon and evening. Colic typically appears when a baby is a few weeks old and usually settles by the time they are around 3 to 4 months old.
How do I know if my baby has colic?

According to NHS guidance, a baby may have colic if they cry for more than 3 hours a day, on more than 3 days a week, for at least one week, while otherwise remaining healthy. Signs during an episode can include clenched fists, a flushed face, drawing the knees up, arching the back, and passing wind.
What can I do to soothe my baby during the witching hour?

The NHS suggests holding and cuddling your baby, keeping them upright during and after feeds, burping them thoroughly, gently rocking them, offering a warm bath, and using soft background noise. There is no strong evidence that anti-colic drops or herbal supplements help.
When should I contact a doctor about my baby's crying?
Contact NHS 111 or your GP if you are worried, if the crying does not ease with the strategies you have tried, if your baby is not gaining weight as expected, or if symptoms carry on beyond 4 months.

d.t: Therapy options for postnatal mental health: what is available and how to access it
q: What is the most effective therapy for postnatal depression?

CBT (cognitive behavioural therapy) and IPT (interpersonal therapy) both have strong evidence for postnatal depression. CBT focuses on the relationship between thoughts, feelings, and behaviours. IPT focuses specifically on the impact of relationships and life transitions on mood. Either is a reasonable starting point; the best approach depends partly on your individual situation and what is available.
Can I access therapy on the NHS for postnatal mental health?

Yes. You can speak to your GP and ask for a referral to a talking therapies service (sometimes called IAPT or NHS Talking Therapies). In most areas you can also self-refer without going through your GP. Waiting times vary by area. If your needs are complex or severe, ask about referral to a specialist perinatal mental health team.
What is EMDR and when is it used?

EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing) is a therapy with strong evidence for PTSD. It involves processing traumatic memories using bilateral stimulation, typically eye movements guided by a therapist. It is used for birth trauma and other trauma in the perinatal period. It is available through some NHS services and many private therapists.
What is PANDAS Foundation?

PANDAS Foundation is a UK charity providing support for parents with perinatal mental illness. They offer a helpline, peer support groups, and online resources. Their helpline number is 0808 1961 776 (freephone). They can provide support alongside professional treatment.
How do I choose a private therapist for postnatal mental health?

Look for a therapist who is registered with a recognised professional body (BACP, UKCP, or BPS in the UK). If possible, look for someone with specific experience in perinatal mental health. It is reasonable to ask prospective therapists about their experience with postnatal issues before beginning. A good fit between you and the therapist matters as much as their qualifications.
Is online therapy as effective as in-person therapy?

For most common presentations including postnatal depression and anxiety, online therapy has been found to be comparably effective to in-person therapy. For parents of young babies, online delivery can be more accessible and easier to fit around feeding and nap schedules. Some people still prefer in-person work, and for trauma, some therapists prefer to work in person. Both are valid.

d.t: Toddler aggression at playgroup: handling biting and hitting in social settings
q: My child only bites at playgroup, never at home. Why?

Group settings are significantly more demanding on a toddler's regulatory system than the home environment. At home, the space is familiar, resources are plentiful, and the pace is shaped by the child's own rhythm. At playgroup, all of that changes at once. The biting is a regulation problem specific to a particular set of conditions, not a character problem.
How do I apologise to the parent of a child my toddler bit?

Directly and simply: say you are sorry and that you know it must have been upsetting. Do not minimise what happened, but do not spiral into excessive shame. Following up with how you are actively addressing it, if asked, is appropriate. Most parents understand that toddler biting is a developmental thing, even if they are shaken in the moment.
Should my toddler be banned from playgroup after biting?

Exclusion is rarely an effective or appropriate response to developmental aggression at this age. A consistent, calm, brief response combined with antecedent management is far more useful. If the playgroup is considering exclusion, it may be worth discussing a supported reduced-attendance plan with clear goals for return to full participation.
My toddler bites the same child every time. What does that mean?

There may be a specific dynamic between the two children that consistently tips your child's regulation. The other child may play loudly, compete for the same toys, or move into personal space in a way that repeatedly overwhelms yours. Managing their proximity while working on regulation skills is a practical short-term approach.
Is my toddler going to be aggressive forever?

Almost certainly not. Physical aggression in group settings peaks in the 18- to 30-month window and declines sharply as language develops and the prefrontal cortex matures. With consistent responses and appropriate support, the vast majority of children have resolved group aggression well before age 4.
The playgroup leader said my child needs to be disciplined more firmly. How do I respond?

Acknowledge their concern and thank them for raising it. You can gently share that brief, consistent responses and antecedent management are more effective than prolonged corrections. Ask if they can work with you on a consistent whole-room response. If the environment continues to feel unsupportive, it is entirely reasonable to try a different group.

d.t: Toddler defiance: why they say no to everything and what to do about it
q: My toddler says no even to things they want to do. Is that normal?

Yes. The "no" reflex becomes so strong at this stage that it can fire before the toddler has fully processed what was asked. Waiting a moment after the initial refusal, or gently rephrasing the offer, often produces a different answer. The toddler is not being contrary on purpose. The impulse is faster than the thinking.
Is giving choices spoiling a toddler?

No. Choices within clear boundaries build autonomy without removing structure. Spoiling is typically about the absence of boundaries or the immediate gratification of every demand. Offering a choice between two acceptable options is the opposite of that. It gives the child agency within a framework, which is developmentally healthy.
My toddler has a full meltdown when I override a no. How do I handle it?

Stay calm and hold the boundary. Empathise with the feeling without giving in to the demand: "I hear that you really did not want that, and we still need to go." The meltdown is the toddler's emotional system responding to disappointment. The appropriate response is warmth and steadiness, not capitulation.
How many choices should I offer per day?

There is no set number. The aim is to consistently include the toddler in decisions where there are real options available. The goal is for the child to experience regular agency throughout the day, not to hit a specific count. Some days will naturally offer more opportunities than others.
My child cooperates at nursery but refuses everything at home. Why?

This is very common and is, in a meaningful sense, a compliment to your relationship. Children save their hardest emotions for their safest people. At nursery they are on best behaviour partly because the relationship is not yet safe enough to fall apart in. At home, they know they can. It does not mean you are doing anything wrong.
At what age does the "no" phase ease?

The intensity typically peaks somewhere between 18 and 24 months and begins to ease by 3 to 4 years as language develops and the child gains more legitimate channels for autonomy. The defiance does not disappear, but it becomes more manageable and more negotiable over time.

d.t: Toddler emotional regulation: what it is, why it takes years, and how you help
q: Should I send my toddler to their room to calm down?

A quiet space can help some children who willingly seek it. However, sending a distressed toddler away from their safe person usually adds an experience of abandonment to the existing distress. Staying close and calm while they work through the feeling is generally more effective than removal.
My toddler's big emotions are exhausting me. Is that normal?

Yes, fully. Co-regulation takes a real toll on the parent's nervous system. The reason you find it draining is that you are genuinely regulating with your child. Your own rest, support, and nervous system health matter just as much as any technique.
Are boys harder to regulate emotionally than girls?

There is no meaningful neurological difference in emotional regulation capacity by gender at toddler age. Cultural expectations shape how emotional expression is responded to. Boys who are shamed for crying often have fewer tools as a result, not because of biology.
My toddler has big meltdowns but recovers very quickly. Is that okay?

Yes, this is often healthy. The ability to recover quickly suggests good elasticity. The intensity of the meltdown in these years is about emotional volume, not evidence of lasting damage or dysfunction.
When should I expect my child to be able to start self-regulating?

Very early steps emerge around age 3 to 4. Basic self-soothing strategies appear then, though they are inconsistent. Genuine self-regulation develops across childhood and adolescence. Even adults rely on co-regulation from others under significant stress.
Is it possible to spoil a toddler by responding to every big emotion?

No. Consistent, warm responses to emotional distress build secure attachment, which is the foundation of all later self-regulation. Responding to emotional needs is different from giving in to demands. The distinction matters, and the research is clear that responsiveness supports, not undermines, independence.

d.t: Toddler grazing vs structured meals: why the routine actually matters
q: How often should a toddler eat?

Toddlers have small stomachs and high energy needs relative to their body size, which means they genuinely need to eat frequently. A schedule of three meals and two to three planned snacks, spaced roughly two to three hours apart, works well for most toddlers aged 1 to 3 years. This gives enough time between eating for genuine hunger to build before the next opportunity.
My toddler says they are hungry right after a meal. What should I do?

This is very common. The most straightforward response is to calmly say that the kitchen is closed and the next snack or meal will be at a specific time. Hold the boundary warmly and without drama. If your toddler genuinely ate very little at the meal, it is worth reflecting on whether the meal was offered at a time when hunger was already low due to a recent snack. Adjusting snack timing often reduces post-meal requests for more food.
How is structured snacking different from grazing?

Structured snacking means offering snacks at set times, with a clear beginning and end to the eating opportunity, and nothing in between except water. Grazing means food is available more or less continuously and eating happens whenever the child asks. The key difference is whether there is a hunger-building gap between eating occasions. Structured snacks function like mini-meals and allow a proper hunger cycle to develop.
What should I offer at a snack versus a meal?

Meals tend to be more nutritionally complete, combining a protein, a starchy carbohydrate, vegetables or fruit, and a dairy or dairy-equivalent food.
